Abstract

We present Denario, an AI multi-agent system designed to serve as a scientific research assistant. Denario can perform many different tasks, such as generating ideas, checking the literature, developing research plans, writing and executing code, making plots, and drafting and reviewing a scientific paper. The system has a modular architecture, allowing it to handle specific tasks, such as generating an idea, or carrying out end-to-end scientific analysis using Cmbagent as a deep-research backend. In this work, we describe in detail Denario and its modules, and illustrate its capabilities by presenting multiple AI-generated papers generated by it in many different scientific disciplines such as astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, material science, mathematical physics, medicine, neuroscience and planetary science. Denario also excels at combining ideas from different disciplines, and we illustrate this by showing a paper that applies methods from quantum physics and machine learning to astrophysical data. We report the evaluations performed on these papers by domain experts, who provided both numerical scores and review-like feedback. We then highlight the strengths, weaknesses, and limitations of the current system. Finally, we discuss the ethical implications of AI-driven research and reflect on how such technology relates to the philosophy of science. We publicly release the code at this URL. A Denario demo can also be run directly on the web at this URL, and the full app will be deployed on the cloud.

### 1 Introduction

Modern science has been built on the rules of the scientific method [1]. This empirical and iterative method begins by formulating an idea or hypothesis, which represents the foundation for the entire research endeavor. This initial idea might arise from a variety of sources: a theoretical question, an unexplained phenomenon, an unexpected result in prior work, or a curiosity-driven exploration of a dataset or simulation. The hypothesis can aim to explain an observed behavior in nature, test the validity of a theoretical model, or uncover new patterns or relationships within existing data.

Once the idea is identified, it is often refined through collaboration discussions, preliminary literature reviews, and feasibility assessments. Researchers seek to understand the broader context of the problem, what has already been studied, and where the current knowledge gaps lie. This step is crucial for ensuring that the proposed work is novel, feasible, and impactful.

Next, a detailed plan is developed to execute the project and investigate the proposed idea. This stage involves identifying the necessary data, selecting or designing appropriate methodologies, and outlining the sequence of steps required for the analysis. Depending on the nature of the research, this may include data collection or simulation, data preprocessing and cleaning, implementing algorithms or analytical models, and performing statistical or computational analyses. Along this process, scientists may use lower-dimensional representations of the data, e.g., via plots or diagrams, to help interpret intermediate

results and to communicate findings effectively. The ultimate goal of this phase is to systematically explore the hypothesis, extract meaningful insights, and arrive at scientifically sound conclusions.

Finally, a scientific paper or report is written describing in detail the problem or hypothesis, the methods used, the results obtained, and the conclusions reached, describing how the research has advanced knowledge and its connections with previous works.

Each of the above steps is a highly sophisticated task that requires extensive time for highly skilled domain experts. Because of this, the generation of a scientific paper can take from months to years. Unfortunately, a significant fraction of that time is consumed on tasks such as literature search, learning new methods, debugging code, and writing text. These are tasks where recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), such as large language models and AI agents, can help. Thus, developing AI tools that can assist scientists with some or all of the tasks involved in the generation of new knowledge can accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to formulate new hypotheses and test those faster than in the traditional method.

In this work, we introduce and describe Denario, an AI multi-agent system designed to serve as a scientific research assistant. Denario can generate ideas, check the literature to evaluate the novelty of those, develop research plans, write and execute code, make plots, and draft and review scientific papers. It can also perform end-to-end scientific research by carrying out, sequentially, all the above tasks. We evaluate the capabilities and limitations of Denario by generating paper drafts from a very diverse set of disciplines, from biology to astrophysics, and reporting the positive and negative aspects of these papers, as judged by domain experts. Hoping to be a tool that can accelerate scientific discovery, we also make Denario publicly available.

We want to stress that Denario is not the first attempt at building tools to help researchers perform end-to-end research. The idea of having machines perform research is much older. For instance, the robot scientist (also known as Adam) [2] was able to formulate hypotheses, plan and run experiments (physically via robotics), interpret the results, and repeat the cycle. Adam was designed to study functional genomics and was the first machine to generate scientific knowledge independently of humans. The same group later developed Eve [3], another robot scientist tailored towards drug discovery. Another early important work is the Automated Statistician [4], which was able to perform a detailed statistical analysis of some data and provide a report about its findings. More recently, lots of recent work on AI assistants for research has been done by many different teams, such as Sakana AI-scientist [5, 6], Google co-scientist [7], AI-cosmologist [8], Curie [9], and Agent laboratory [10].

We note that lots of works are also developing tools to help scientists with increasingly sophisticated tasks. For instance, AutoWEKA was developed to identify the best machine learning model to tackle a particular problem [11]. ResearchAgent [12] was able to formulate new hypotheses and design experiments by checking their novelty with the literature. [13] created a self-driving lab to re-engineer enzymes without human intervention, while [14] created a virtual lab with several AI-scientist experts in different areas capable of creating nanobodies. Another example is AstroAgents [15], a multi-agent system designed to test and consolidate many different hypotheses about the origins of life on Earth. Recent works have also shown that AI systems can write expert-level scientific software and discover new algorithms [16, 17, 18]. Other works are exploring the capabilities of agentic systems via graphs [19, 20]. We also note that AgentRxiv [21] is a framework for Agents to learn from previous works.

While some of these technologies have the potential to accelerate scientific discovery –for instance, [22] designed an autonomous system combining AI with robotics to discover new materials a lot of serious debates about human standards for validation sparked [23]. These are very important considerations and we discuss them in detail, for the case of Denario. Furthermore, given the ethical considerations raised by such a technology, we devote a paper section to discuss ethical aspects, along with how this technology fits within the philosophy of science.

We note that in scientific research, there is usually a tradeoff between depth and breadth, given a fixed amount of time to carry out a task or study. We believe that AI systems like Denario can help researchers explore a wide range of possibilities, at a more superficial level, while researchers can go deeper into the most interesting or promising ones. We emphasize that the goal of Denario is not to automate science, but to develop a research assistant that can accelerate scientific discovery. By making Denario publicly available and user-friendly, we hope it will become a standard tool that benefits the scientific community in their enterprises.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the different pieces that made our system, such as LLMs, AI agents, and agentic orchestration. In Sec. 3 we describe in detail the different modules in Denario and show the different ways to run the system in Sec. 4. In Sec. 5, we show different AIgenerated papers from many different disciplines and discuss the positive and negative aspects of those.

We then present in Sec. 6 some of the observed failure modes of Denario together with advantages, limitations, and future directions. We discuss the ethical considerations that systems like Denario raise and how the technology powering is seen from the philosophy of science in Sec. 7. We conclude in Sec. 8.

### 2 AI multi-agent systems

Denario is an AI multi-agent framework designed to function as a scientific research assistant. It is built with AG2 and LangGraph, and designed to assist in different stages of the research process. It can also execute multiple tasks sequentially, enabling it to perform end-to-end scientific research.

The system is composed of several modules, each focused on a specific task. Within each module, there are agents—autonomous or semi-autonomous computational entities that perceive their environment, process information, and take actions to achieve defined goals. Some of these are AI agents, which leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform specialized tasks. Agents can communicate and collaborate to solve complex problems, while orchestration manages their interactions—determining task order, information flow, and overall coordination. The system takes some input text and returns one or several outputs depending on how Denario is run. We show a cartoon representation of the system in Fig. 1.

In this section, we describe the different components relevant to setting the agents, including the LLM models and the orchestration.

##### 2.1 Large Language Models

The majority of the agents in Denario are AI-agents that typically call Large Language Models (LLMs) [24], including multi-modal ones, with a very specialized prompt that may depend on the output of other agents. Denario allows the user to choose among many different models, including:

- • gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, gpt-4o, gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, o3-mini from OpenAI,
- • gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.5-flash, gemini-2.0-flash from Google,

- • claude-3-7-sonnet, claude-4-Opus, claude-4.1-Opus, claude-4.5 from Anthropic.

We note that Denario is not limited to these LLMs, and new models, or models from other providers, can easily be incorporated into the system. Our choice of models has so far been made based on trial and error rather than systematic evaluation. For example, for coding, our primary models of choice are gemini-2.5-pro, gpt-4.1, and o3-mini. For critiquing and reviewing, our default choice is Claude models or reasoning models from OpenAI.

##### 2.2 Multi-Agent Orchestration and Strategy

In Denario, the agent orchestration is carried out with two different frameworks: AG21 and LangGraph2. Some modules (e.g. idea module) are implemented in both frameworks, while others (e.g. analysis module) are only implemented in one framework. Some modules implemented in AG2 follow the Planning & Control strategy as implemented in Cmbagent that we describe below.

###### 2.2.1 Orchestration

- • AG2. AG2 is an open-source AgentOS that supports advanced agentic AI applications and research. It offers an agentic abstraction that unifies AI foundation models like LLMs, non-LLM tools and human inputs, and intuitive conversation programming to orchestrate multiple agents. Stronger agents or agentic systems can be composed recursively using primitive agents and basic conversation patterns like sequential chats, group chats, nested chats. This modular architecture also enables rich agentic design patterns such as advanced tool use, structured context, conditional handoffs, dynamic updates, dynamic task decomposition and team building, guardrails, and many other extensions. All agents using AG2 are part of Cmbagent [25, 26, 27], an open source and publicly available3 multi-agent system designed to perform a variety of scientific research-related tasks.
- • LangGraph. LangGraph is based on LangChain4 and is an open-source Python framework designed to orchestrate agents through directed graphs. In LangGraph, the graph nodes represent callable units, such as agents, functions, and tools. The edges between nodes represent the way the flow of the computation is carried out. Another important component of LangGraph is the graph state, an object (typically a Python class) passed through the different nodes and enabling agent communication, memory, coordination, etc. LangGraph supports both static and dynamic graphs. For instance, depending on the outcome of an agent, one may want to call a particular agent. Loops and interrupts are also allowed in LangGraph.

###### 2.2.2 Planning and Control Strategy

Planning & Control, a fundamental concept in robotics, refers to strategies for orchestrating decisionmaking and action execution. The basic idea is that during the planning phase, a complex task is decomposed into smaller, manageable subtasks, and a strategy is defined for achieving them. During the control phase, these subtasks are executed, with monitoring and adjustments as needed to ensure the overall goal is achieved. Some modules in Denario follow this strategy, as implemented in Cmbagent. We now briefly describe the Cmbagent Planning & Control implementation and refer the reader to [26] for further details. The strategy is illustrated in figure 2.

In Cmbagent, during the planning phase, the main task is broken down into sub-tasks, and an agent is assigned to each of them. During control, the agent responsible for a sub-task executes its instructions until completion. Once a sub-task is complete, a control agent records its status and proceeds to the next sub-task, continuing until the entire plan is complete.

The Planning stage starts with a call to a plan setter agent, whose task is to select the set of agents that should be involved during the session. This function call stores into the context detailed instructions for the plan (namely, the agents and description of agents that should be involved) and ends on the next agent target, which is the planner agent. Then, the elaboration of a plan is done via a two-agent conversation where a planner agent suggests plans and a plan reviewer agent suggests recommendations on the plan. Recommendations and suggested plans are recorded in the context via function calls, including the number of steps in the plan. This information is injected into each agent’s

- Figure 2: Planning & Control implementation of “Deep Research” from Cmbagent. This is the essential orchestration strategy enabling the research analysis without human-in-the-loop. Additionally, it can be used for idea generation, method generation and data pre-processing.

system message before reply. The number of review rounds, nreviews, is a hyperparameter of our system, and we generally set it to one5. Once the number of rounds of recommendation nreviews is reached, the final plan is recorded into the context, and the Planning stage ends. The response of the planner is a list of subtasks, where each subtask consists of three fields:

- • sub task: the sub-task to be performed

- • sub task agent: the name of the agent in charge of the sub-task.

- • bullet points: A bullet-point list describing the specific actions the subtask is expected to perform.

The number of subtasks is constrained from the prompt of the planner and plan reviewer agents, which are instructed to produce a plan with, at most, nsteps steps, another tunable hyperparameter of our system. Typically, our plans contain between 3 and 8 steps6.

The Control stage is orchestrated by a control agent. The plan obtained from the Planning stage is injected into the system message of the control agent and it replies by calling the record status function. This function updates the context variable dictionary to record the current step being executed, whether it is completed, failed, or in progress, whether some new plots or new code have been produced, whether some code execution has failed, and, depending on this information, which agent to transfer to next. The control agent records two types of termination signals: whether the number of times a code execution has failed exceeds the maximum number of failures allowed by the user, or whether the final step of the plan has been carried out successfully. In the former, the session aborts before the main task has been solved, and in the latter, the session ends positively with the full plan completely executed. Upon reception of a termination signal, control agent transfers to a terminator agent to end the session smoothly.

Given the fact that the system may fall into an infinite loop (e.g., trying unsuccessfully to fix a bug), we set a hard limit to the maximum number of messages exchanged between the agents, nrounds. By

5With more rounds, we often observe that the suggested plans become overly complex and ineffective. 6As the context passed to the agents tends to grow during a session, a plan with more steps will generally lead to a more

default, we set this to nrounds = 500. The system will fail if more than nrounds are exchanged. We note the system can fail for many other reasons, including limits on API calls set on the provider platforms, or occasional exceptions/errors that are not fully dealt with.

For instance, Denario can be run as a standalone program and generate a paper from the input text file (by running the idea, methods, analysis, and paper modules sequentially), or can also be used as a standalone tool to create plots and results from an input text, idea, and methods provided by the user.

For most of the modules, Denario requires an input text guiding the system’s behavior. This text can contain the description of the data to be used together with some computational constraints. It can also simply contain a description of a problem to be solved. For some research applications, it can also be relevant to specify that the data can (or should) be generated by the agents. The six main modules in Denario can perform these tasks (see Table 1 for a summary):

- • Idea module. This module is in charge of generating an idea for a project. This module only requires the input text file to be run. After calling this module, Denario will print out the idea and save it in a markdown file called idea.md. The agents in charge of this module are described in Section 3.2.
- • Literature module. This module is in charge of checking the literature to figure out if an idea is original or there are existing works that have carried it out. The input to this module is the input text together with the idea.md file. This module will then check the literature and and write a report on whether the idea is new or not. The report will be saved to a file called literature.md. The agents in charge of this module are described in Section 3.3.

|Module<br><br>|Task|Input|Output|
|---|---|---|---|

|Idea<br><br>|Generate project idea|input.md<br><br>|idea.md|
|---|---|---|---|
|Literature|Determine if idea is new|input.md idea.md<br><br>|literature.md|
|Methods<br><br>|Develop project plan|input.md idea.md|methods.md|
|Analysis|Implement plan write and execute code make plots<br><br>|input.md idea.md methods.md|results.md Plots<br><br>|
|Paper<br><br>|Write paper<br><br>|input.md idea.md methods.md results.md|paper.pdf|
|Review|Review paper<br><br>|(input.md) paper.pdf|referee.md|

Table 1: This table shows the different modules contained in Denario along with their tasks, inputs, and outputs. input.md contains a description of the data or problem of interest and is provided by the human researcher in markdown format. idea.md contains the project idea, literature.md a report on whether the idea is new, methods.md the research methodology, results.md the research analysis, Plots is a folder containing the plots and referee.md contains a referee report. paper.pdf is the scientific paper in pdf format. Files between parentheses are optional.

- • Methodology module. This module is in charge of generating a detailed plan to carry out the idea. To be run, it needs the input description text file and the idea.md file with the description of the idea. We note that idea.md can be generated by the previous module or provided by the user. After executing this module, Denario generates a detailed plan outlining the steps and methods needed for the project. Denario stores this generated text in a file called methods.md. The agents in this module are described in Section 3.4
- • Analysis module. This module is in charge of implementing the research plan. It requires the input text, together with the idea.md and methods.md files (generated by previous modules or provided by the user). By calling this module, Denario will carry out the research plan, usually translating into writing and running code, making plots, etc. The output of this module is a file, results.md, with the outcome of the analysis, together with the plots generated. The agents behind this module are described in Section 3.5.
- • Paper module. This module is in charge of writing a scientific paper. This module requires the input text along with the idea.md, methods.md, results.md, and all plots. As above, these files can be the outcome of the modules or can be provided by the user. By calling this module, Denario writes a scientific paper and saves the .tex, .bib, and .pdf files. The agents behind this module are described in Section 3.6.
- • Review module. This module is in charge of reviewing a scientific paper. The input to this module is a pdf with the scientific paper along with an input description (optional). This module will review the paper and provide a report about the positive and negative aspects of the draft. The output of this module is a referee report that will be saved on a file called referee.md. The agents behind this module are described in Section 3.7.

We emphasize that Denario is designed in a modular way. By calling sequentially all the above modules, Denario will perform end-to-end scientific research from an input text (e.g. from a description of a dataset). However, the user can also just run one (or several) of the modules to perform a specific task. For instance, given a well-defined idea and research plan (provided by the user), the user can run the analysis module to write code and create plots. We now discuss in detail the architecture and agents involved in each module of Denario.

##### 3.1 Input Text

All modules in Denario accept an input text. This input text usually contains a description of the data to be analyzed or the problem to be solved. This text is later used by the modules to generate ideas,

develop research plans, analyze the data, or check the literature. How well the system behaves depends critically on this text. We now outline a few guidelines on how to write the input text:

- • If the project to carry out consists of analyzing some data, and the structure of the dataset is not well described, the analysis module will fail, as the code it will write will likely not be appropriate to read the data properly. We recommend that the user describe the data or the problem with as much detail as possible in the input text. For instance, if the project is about analyzing a tabular dataset, it is important to write what the data is about and some context. Besides, it is important to describe in detail what the different columns and rows are, and specify things like units, ranges (if available), etc.
- • If the goal is not to analyze some data but instead to solve some problem, it is very important to describe in detail the problem, connections with previous works, and some details about the steps to carry out if known.
- • It is also very important to write explicitly the location of the data (with absolute paths if possible); otherwise, the system will not be able to find the location of the data.
- • When used in end-to-end mode, Denario sometimes may generate papers with very few plots. One can fix this by writing in the input text to generate many plots for each step. Sometimes, the system may generate many similar plots, which will make the paper more like a research note than an actual paper. For this, the user can add some text like this: Join plots that are similar.
- • We have also seen cases where Denario fails to read the data, and to continue, it will create its own synthetic one. To avoid these situations, we usually write in the input text Do not create dummy data..
- • One can also set computational constraints in the input text so that the system is aware of what resources it has when performing the analysis. Examples of this are: You have access to 1 GPU and 10 CPUs; use all the resources when training neural networks.
- • We have observed cases where the system is not able to use a particular library (perhaps because it does not know about its documentation or because its API has recently changed). In these cases, the user can explicitly write Do not use X library to perform this analysis to avoid that situation.
- • On the other hand, if the user has some piece of code, or a library, that may not be known to LLMs, the user can add instructions about its usage in the input text so that the system learns how to use it when analyzing the data.
- • In many occasions, it is necessary to iterate over the input text in order to guide the system in a particular direction or to improve the quality of the generated papers. In this case, the user should add details about previous experiments, or directions where the analysis is wanted, in order to achieve the desired outcome.
- • If arXiv URL’s are provided in the input text description, Denario automatically downloads the pdf of the corresponding papers. The pdf’s are OCR’ed with mistral ocr lattest and the resulting markdown versions are stored in the local repository. Then, the full markdown versions are sent to o3-mini for summarization and the summary of the papers are appended to the initial input text, providing the necessary contextual information for the subsequent LLM agents. (In the GUI this is done with the Enhance data description button, see Fig. 9.)

We refer the reader to the example papers repository7 for a comprehensive list of examples, across disciplines, of input text used for different papers.

##### 3.2 Idea module

The goal of this module is to generate research ideas given some input text (e.g. describing some dataset). We note that recent work [28] has suggested that AI-generated ideas may be more novel (according to human evaluators), than human-generated ideas. The input to this module is the input text (see Fig. 3) and the output of it is a file called idea.md that stores the generated idea. We now describe in detail how this module works.

7https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioExamplePapers

[Figure 3]

- Figure 4: The Idea module is a propose-critique block consisting of two agents: idea maker and idea hater. The system first calls the idea maker agent, that will generate an idea given the input text. Next, the idea is sent to the idea hater, who will critique the generated idea. The idea maker will then take the input text, the generated idea, and the critique and will improve the idea. This process is then repeated several times until the final idea is generated.

A critical part of scientific research is the generation and refinement of ideas. In any ambitious project, it’s not enough to simply work on a fixed plan – creativity and adaptability are needed to explore the best possible directions. However, creativity must be balanced by careful critique to ensure ideas are realistic, impactful, and tightly connected to the available data. To systematize this process, our pipeline includes specialized agents dedicated to idea generation (idea maker) and idea critique (idea hater).

In this pipeline, the idea maker agent generates creative and feasible research project ideas based on the input text and any feedback from the idea hater agent. Its goal is to propose diverse approaches for extracting new information, considering the current plan, task, and instructions. However, simply generating ideas is not enough – to ensure that only the strongest, most relevant ideas move forward, each proposal must undergo careful evaluation. This is where the idea hater agent steps in, critically reviewing each idea for feasibility, scientific value, and relevance to the dataset. By identifying weaknesses and suggesting improvements, the idea hater ensures that no idea is accepted blindly without scrutiny.

- Figure 4 provides a schematic of the conversation between the idea maker and idea hater agents. This loop can be repeated as many times as requested.

This setup mirrors the natural human process of idea development, where individuals brainstorm concepts and refine them through feedback and discussion. Just like in human teams, iteration is key: the idea maker improves its proposals based on the critiques received from the idea hater, leading to a cycle of continuous refinement. This multi-agent dialogue helps distill raw ideas into well-formed, robust research directions, ultimately ensuring that the final projects are both innovative and grounded in realistic scientific practice. The concept of multi-agent systems to produce ideas has been motivated by previous works such as [29], who used reinforcement learning between agents, and [30], who showed that a large team of agents produced better ideas than a single agent. In its current version, Denario has two different implementations (see Section 2.2) for this module:

- • Fast idea. In this case, a single idea is generated by the idea maker agent and then improved (or completely changed) after receiving feedback from the idea hater agent. The final idea is obtained after three iterations of the two agents, followed by a further iteration from the idea maker agent. This implementation is fast (around 15 seconds with gemini-2.0-flash) and is written in LangGraph.

- • Planning & Control idea. This implementation is carried out with Cmbagent using the planning and control strategy. The instructions passed to the Planning agents are:

Idea Generation Planning Instructions Given these datasets and information, make a plan according to the following instructions:

- 1. Ask idea maker to generate 5 new research project ideas related to the datasets.

- 2. Ask idea hater to critique these ideas.

- 3. Ask idea maker to select and improve 2 out of the 5 research project ideas given the output of the idea hater.

- 4. Ask idea hater to critique the 2 improved ideas.

- 5. Ask idea maker to select the best idea from the two.

- 6. Ask idea maker to report the best idea as a scientific paper title, accompanied by a 5-sentence description.

The goal of this task is to generate a research project idea based on the data of interest. Don’t suggest performing any calculations or analyses here. The only goal of this task is to obtain the best possible project idea.

During the Planning stage, the planner and plan reviewer design the plan for the idea maker and idea hater agents to generate an idea, given the input text needed for the module. To illustrate this implementation, we show below the first two steps of an idea generation plan created by using as input text a description of the Perovskite database [31]:

Idea Generation Plan Example (First 2 Steps Only) Sub-task: Generate 5 new research project ideas related to the perovskite dataset.

Agent: idea maker Instructions:

- • Review the dataset description and attributes.
- • Propose 5 innovative and feasible research project ideas based on the dataset’s scope and potential.
- • Ensure the ideas are diverse and cover different aspects of the dataset.
- • Consider focusing on different aspects such as material composition relationships, fabrication parameters, device architecture correlations, stability factors, and performance optimization based on the 95 attributes in the dataset.

Sub-task: Critique the 5 research project ideas. Agent: idea hater Instructions:

- • Evaluate the feasibility, originality, and potential impact of each idea.
- • Identify weaknesses or limitations in the ideas.
- • Suggest improvements or recommend discarding weak ideas.
- • Evaluate each idea’s scientific novelty and whether it leverages the unique comprehensive nature of this manually curated dataset with 42,400+ devices.

As seen in this example, with this approach, the idea maker and idea hater agents receive explicit instructions specific to the data or problem of interest. This could potentially improve the quality of the generated ideas. However, this approach is time-consuming and incurs a significant cost. With our default LLM choices (we use gpt-4o and claude-3-7-sonnet for idea maker and idea hater, respectively), Planning takes ∼1 minute and costs ∼ $0.20, while Control takes ∼3 minutes and costs ∼ $0.90. This amounts to ∼ $1 and ∼ 4 minutes per generated idea, to be contrasted with the 15 seconds of the fast method that comes at no or significantly lower cost with gemini-2.0-flash.

The reason behind the two different implementations of this module is to provide the user more flexibility when using Denario. For instance, a new user may prefer to use the fast idea implementation to get results quicker, while in full production mode, the user may prefer a more robust approach by using the curated idea generation.

As stated above, this module will generate an idea and store it in a file called idea.md. This file is later used as input for other modules. We emphasize that the user can use the idea module to generate an idea, or can provide the idea directly by writing it to the idea.md file.

##### 3.3 Literature module

The goal of the literature module is to search the literature to determine whether an idea, in combination with the input text, is new or not. This module takes as input the input text together with the idea (usually in the form of the idea.md file). The module then searches the literature for papers similar to the proposed idea and evaluates whether the project idea is new or not. The input text is taken into consideration when evaluating the idea. We do this because in some research areas, standard techniques applied to new datasets may be seen as novel research. For instance, even if graph neural networks are very standard in deep learning, they may not have been applied to cosmological datasets, and this may be seen as novel in the cosmology research area. The module returns a file, literature.md, that contains a report on whether the idea is new or not. Denario provides two different implementations of this module:

[Figure 4]

- Figure 5: This diagram shows the semantic scholar implementation of the literature module. The module takes as input the input text and the idea. These files are then passed to a novelty agent whose task is to determine if the idea is new or not. This agent can output 1) idea new, 2) idea not new, or 3) query. The agent will choose the later if it does not enough information to make a yes/no decision. In that case, it will generate a query that will be sent to the semantic scholar agent who will search the literature with it. This agent will then retrieve a series of papers (including titles and abstracts) and will send this information back to the novelty agent. This process is repeated several times until the relevant literature is well sampled. If no relevant papers are found after a number of iterations, the novelty agent will conclude that the idea is new. Once the novelty agent has determined that the idea is new/not new, all the papers found, the queries, and the responses will be sent to a summary agent that will write a report stating why the idea is new (or not new) and the most relevant papers.

• Semantic scholar. In this implementation, carried out with LangGraph, we follow the workflow introduced in [5]. The module consist of two agents that collaborate to determine whether an idea, together with the associated data description, is new or has already been carried out. First, the novelty agent is presented with the idea, the data description, and with titles and abstracts of papers already found. The goal of this agent is then to determine whether, with the given information, the paper is new, is not new, or whether it does not have enough information to reach a conclusion. If it determines that the paper is new, or not new, all the information is sent to another agent to summarize the results and to write a report. This report will be placed on a file called literature.md. If the novelty agent determines that it does not have enough information, then it can call the semantic scholar agent which can make a query using Semantic Scholar8. This other agent will then make an API call to Semantic Scholar, using the query sent by the novelty agent, and obtain papers (titles, abstracts, URLs, etc) that will be sent back to the

8https://www.semanticscholar.org/

novelty agent for evaluation. This procedure is repeated several times up to a maximum number, where the module will determine that the idea is new as it has not found relevant papers after multiple iterations. We show a scheme about the workflow of this implementation in Fig. 5.

• FuturHouse’s Owl. For this implementation, we just make use of the Owl agent developed by FutureHouse.9 This is a specialized agent designed to search the literature and provide an answer to the question: Has anyone implemented this idea before? We refer the reader to the FuturHouse documentation10 for details about this agent.

Denario contains both implementations to allow the user to choose among the two, or perhaps better, to run both of them to get to ”independent” opinions. This module will generate the literature report, located in the literature.md file. We note that in the current implementation, this file is not used by any other module. We do this intentionally so that a human evaluator decides whether the idea is truly new/original or not.

##### 3.4 Methods module

[Figure 5]

Figure 6: The methods module.

The methods module is responsible for producing a detailed plan, or methodology, to carry out the project idea. This module takes the input text and the project idea (usually located in the idea.md file), as input. The module’s outcome is a detailed research plan designed to carry out the idea. This output is saved in a file called methods.md. The current version of Denario contains two different implementations for this module:

• Fast methods. This is a simple implementation that takes the input text and the idea.md file and generates a methodology. It is implemented in LangGraph and designed to be run with fast models like gemini-2.5-flash (although it supports most LLMs). The prompt used in this case is this:

Fast methods prompt

You are provided with an input text and an idea for a scientific paper. Your task is to think about the methods to use in order to carry it out. Follow these instructions:

- – Generate a detailed description of the methodology that will be used to perform the research project.
- – The description should clearly outline the steps, techniques, and rationale derived from the exploratory data analysis (EDA).
- – The focus should be strictly on the methods and workflow for this specific project to be performed. Do not include any discussion of future directions, future work, project

- 9https://www.futurehouse.org/
- 10https://futurehouse.gitbook.io/futurehouse-cookbook/futurehouse-client

extensions, or limitations.

- – The description should be written as if it were a senior researcher explaining to her research assistant how to perform the research necessary for this project.
- – Just provide the methods, do not add a sentence at the beginning saying showing your thinking process

Problem or data description: {Input text}

Idea: {project idea}

Respond with the methods you have generated.

• Planning & Control methods. This mode uses the Planning & Control strategy of Cmbagent, with the researcher agent in charge of the subtasks. The models chosen by default for the researcher agent in this mode are gpt-4.1 or gemini-2.5-pro. The instructions for planning are these:

Methods Module; Planning Instructions

Given these datasets, and information on the features and project idea, we want to design a methodology to implement this idea. The goal of the task is to write a plan that will be used to generate a detailed description of the methodology that will be used to perform the research project.

- • Start by requesting the researcher to provide reasoning relevant to the given project idea.
- • Clarify the specific hypotheses, assumptions, or questions that should be investigated.
- • This can be done in multiple steps.
- • The focus should be strictly on the methods and workflow for this specific project to be performed. Do not include any discussion of future directions, future work, project extensions, or limitations.
- • The description should be written as if it were a senior researcher explaining to her research assistant how to perform the research necessary for this project.

The final step of the plan must be entirely dedicated to writing the full Methodology description. The only agent involved in this workflow is the researcher. In this task, we do not perform any calculations or analyses, only outline the methodology.

For this task, the researcher agent of Cmbagent is further instructed as follows: Methods Generation Appended Researcher Instructions

Given this information, we want to design a methodology to implement this idea. The goal of the task is to develop a detailed methodology that will be used to carry out the research project.

- • You should focus on the methods for this specific project to be performed. Do not include any discussion of future directions, future work, project extensions, or limitations.
- • The methodology description should be written as if it were a senior researcher explaining to her research assistant how to perform the project.

The designed methodology should focus on describing the research and analysis that will be performed. The full methodology description should be written in markdown format and include all the details of the designed methodology. It should be roughly 500 words long.

These instructions are appended to the default instructions of the researcher agent. We further constrain nsteps = 4 (maximum 4 steps in the plan). With the default models, at the time of writing this paper, Planning typically costs around $0.20 and takes around 1 minute, while Control takes around 1.5 minutes per step at a cost of around $0.10 per step. Thus, with Planning & Control, the total cost of designing the methodology is around $0.50 and takes around 4 minutes. This is to be contrasted with the Fast mode that takes around 15 seconds at no cost to produce the methodology with gemini-2.0-flash. We note that using gemini-2.5-pro for the fast implementation has a small cost (around ∼ $0.10) and will take around 90 seconds, but typically will produce a much more detailed plan to help run the analysis pipeline.

As in the case of the idea module, we provide two different implementations to the user to enhance their range of options when executing this module. We note that the curated implementation may not necessarily yield a better research plan, while its cost and execution time will be significantly higher than the fast option when run with gemini-2.5-pro. However, we recommend the user try both options for the particular case study.

##### 3.5 Analysis module

The goal of this module is to implement the analysis outlined in the methodology. This is done with Cmbagent [25, 26, 27]. The inputs to this module are the input text, the project idea, and the methodology (either created by earlier modules or supplied directly). The output of the module is 1) a report on the results obtained, located in a file called results.md, and 2) a folder called Plots that contains all plots generated. In the current version of Denario, the analysis module relies exclusively on Cmbagent and its Planning & Control strategy for “Deep Research” orchestration, similar in nature to the workflows of agentic tools like Claude Code or Cursor agent mode. See Fig. 2 for an illustration of this strategy.

For the Planning phase, we append the instructions reported hereafter to the planning agents. Analysis Generation Planning Instructions {research idea}

{methodology}

Given these datasets, project idea and methodology, we want to perform the project analysis and generate the results, plots and insights.

The goal is to perform the in-depth research and analysis. The plan must strictly involve only the following agents: {involved agents str}. The goal here is to do the in-depth research and analysis, not an exploratory data analysis.

The final step of the plan, carried out by the researcher agent, must be entirely dedicated to writing the full Results section of the paper or report. If this research project involves code implementation, this final step should report on all the qualitative and quantitative results, interpretations of the plots and key statistics, and references to the plots generated in the previous steps. The final result report will be what will be passed on to the paper writer agents, so all relevant information must be included in the final report (everything else will be discarded).

As we store the full idea and methodology in the context variable dictionary, the planning instructions contain these explicitly. The context variable involved agents str is a string with the names of the agents involved for the analysis generation, which by default are the engineer and researcher agents of Cmbagent. We append the following instructions to these two agents.

Analysis Generation Appended Engineer Instructions {research idea}

{methodology}

Given these datasets, and information on the features and project idea and methodology, we want to perform the project analysis and generate the results, plots and key statistics. The goal is to perform in-depth research and analysis. This means that you must generate the results, plots, and key statistics.

Warnings for computing and plotting:

- - make sure dynamical ranges are well captured (carefully adjust the limits, binning, and log or linear axes scales, for each feature). For histograms (if needed):
- -Use log-scale for features with values spanning several orders of magnitude.

GENERAL IMPORTANT INSTRUCTIONS: You must print out in the console ALL the quantitative information that you think the researcher will need to interpret the results. (The researcher does not have access to saved data files, only to what you print out!) Remember that the researcher agent can not load information from files, so you must print ALL necessary info in the console (without truncation). For this, it may be necessary to change Pandas (if using it) display options.

The engineer agent is in charge of writing Python code analysis pipelines. The engineer agent call triggers a nested chat (similar to self-debug [32]), of which only the output is kept. This allows for long sessions without hitting LLM provider API token limits. A failed code execution may trigger different transitions. If the number of failed executions is lower than nfails, the module would generally transit back to the engineer agent for another attempt. If the failure is caused by a missing Python package, the system will send a request to an installer agent, which runs a bash pip install command before attempting the code execution again. If the number of failed executions equals nfails, a transition to the terminator agent is triggered and the session ends.

Given the planning instructions reported above, the engineer agent is generally in charge of the bulk of the analysis, while the researcher agent is called in the final step of the workflow to report on the results. For Denario, we append the researcher’ system message with the following instructions:

Analysis Generation Appended Researcher Instructions {research idea}

{methodology}

At the end of the session, your task is to generate a detailed/extensive discussion and interpretation of the results. If quantitative results were derived you should provide interpretations of the plots and interpretations of the key statistics, including reporting meaningful quantitative results, tables and references to material previously generated in the session. The results should be reported in full (not a summary) and in academic style. The results report/section should be around 2000 words. The final result report will be what will be passed on to the paper writer agents, so all relevant information must be included in the final report (everything else will be discarded).

Each step during control, with gemini-2.5-pro or gpt-4.1 as engineer and researcher, costs around $0.30, amounting to around $2 for a plan in 6 steps. The time needed to run this module depends critically on the amount of data, the technique used to analyze it, and the available computational resources. For simple analyses with less than 1 Gigabyte of data, the typical time is ∼30 minutes on a personal computer. The user can (and should) specify which computational resources are ready to be committed to the analysis.

##### 3.6 Paper module

This module is in charge of writing a scientific paper or report. In its current form, it should be seen as a paper draft more than a publication-ready paper. This module is entirely written in LangGraph (but for the keyword search, which uses Cmbagent). The module takes as input the input text, the project idea, the project methodology, and the project results. As for the other modules, these files can be either provided by the user or generated by previous modules. The output of this module is a set of LaTeX files together with associated pdfs. A scheme showing the workflow of this subsystem is shown in Fig. 7. We note that the user has multiple options available when running this module, such as the LLM to use, the journal of the paper, and whether the paper includes citations or not11.

[Figure 6]

- Figure 7: This scheme shows the workflow of the paper writing module. Each node represents an agent (or a group of agents) in charge of a task. The preprocess agent is in charge of reading the input files and performing some basic operations, such as identifying duplicated plots. Later, a series of agents will identify keywords and write different sections of the paper draft. Next, an agent will process the plots, generating captions for them and outputting a preliminary version of the paper draft. Next, an agent will refine the results section to improve references to the plots and to polish the writing on it, generating a second version of the paper draft. Next, an agent will place citations in different sections of the paper, producing a third and fourth final version of the paper draft.

The process starts with an preprocess agent reading the input files, which will be kept in memory until it has finished writing the entire paper. We note that it is easy to include more files in case the paper writing requires more information. For instance, the user may provide an additional file with details about the data, references, literature report, etc. The preprocess agent performs other tasks, such as counting the number of plots, identifying and removing repeating plots, and creating temporary files.

Next, given the texts read above, another agent will select a set of keywords that characterize the paper (see Section 3.6.1). After that, another agent will choose a title for the paper and write the abstract. Next, several agents will write the paper’s different sections: 1) Introduction, 2) Methods, 3) Results, and 4) Conclusions. For each section, an agent is passed the input texts and asked to write the assigned section for the paper. We note that the sections are written sequentially, with each section passed to the next agent to improve the coherence throughout the paper. We perform self-reflections for some sections to improve the quality of the generated text.

Once these sections are written, another agent is asked to take all the plots available and generate captions for them. This is achieved by using the multimodal capabilities of the underlying LLM. We note that the captions are generated taking into account the input files to improve the context and coherence of the captions. Next, another agent is tasked with inserting the figures and their generated captions into the results section. This is done in batches of 7 figures12, as the LLM tends to forget inserting some figures when there are many figures in the prompt. At this point, the system will generate a first LaTeX file, compile it, and generate the corresponding pdf.

After this, another agent is asked to rewrite and polish the results section so that the text describes and refers to the added figures. Next, version 2 of the paper, with the polished results section, will be generated. We do this because we have observed the module failing at this point and we use these versions as checkpoints in case we need to rerun the module.

This module can be run with the option to add citations to the paper. If run in that mode, the text inside the different sections is passed through a Perplexity agent in order to get citations (with arXiv

- 11For research notes or similar, the user may not find it useful to spend time and money adding citations. Given the cost, we tend to add citations only to the papers that have been reviewed and filtered by human experts.
- 12This is in principle a hyperparameter. We have noticed that with current LLMs, including more than 10 figures tends to result in errors, omissions, etc

IDs) to the relevant sentences. We use the Perplexity API with the sonar-reasoning-pro model for this. A script is then used to fetch the BibTeX information from arXiv, which is appended to the LaTeX. At this point, version 3 of the paper is generated and saved to file. Finally, another agent is asked to make a final pass through the different sections of the paper in order to improve the clarity of the text and to fix LaTeX errors. After this, version 4 of the paper is produced.

We note that while multiple agents are always checking for LaTeX errors, and some agents are designed to take the LaTeX errors and fix the text, we find that mistakes can still occur, and that may cause problems with the document compilation. E.g. misplaced citations, tables not displayed properly, problems with symbols like and &, and %. For that reason, the paper writing module does not produce a single version of the paper but four different ones, as progress is made. If a problem arises, and the agents themselves are not able to fix it, then, a human can try to fix it manually from of these checkpoints.

###### 3.6.1 Keyword Search module

Cmbagent provides a method to get the keywords which best characterize a given input text, such as the abstract of a paper. The Denario Paper module makes use of this functionality to find the correspondent keywords of the project by passing as input text the idea and methodology. There are three keyword lists that can be searched by this method:

- • UNESCO Nomenclature. This taxonomy has three levels for classifying science and technology domains, subfields and specific areas. We do the keyword search in four steps. First, the keyword agent is provided with the list of domains (2-digit codes) and is asked to select at most 3 domains. Second, for each selected domain, the keyword agent is asked to select at most 3 subfields. Third, for each subfields, the keyword agent is asked to select 3 specific areas. Domains, subfields and specific areas are aggregated into one list and in the last step the agent is asked to select the N most relevant keywords where N is the number of keywords requested by the user. The original UNESCO document is publicly available.13 In principle, this list of keywords is broad enough to be used in all scientific domains. Nevertheless, it is from 1988 and recent technical vocabulary is sometimes lacking.
- • AAAI Keywords. Here, the keyword agent is provided with the full list of AAAI (The Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence) keywords and asked to select the N most relevant keywords where N is the number of keywords requested by the user. The AAAI list of keywords is publicly available.14 This list is relevant for AI-focused research and is updated yearly.
- • AAS Keywords. The keyword agent is provided with the full AAS (American Astronomical Society) list of keywords and asked to select the N most relevant keywords where N is the number of keywords requested by the user. This list should only be used for astrophysics related papers, and can be consulted in the AAS journal page.15

##### 3.7 Review module

This module is in charge of reviewing the generated paper and providing a report about what is good, interesting, and innovative in the paper, but also about the bad things, flaws, etc. The input to it is a pdf document together with the input text (optional). The module will then break down the paper into a set of images, one image for each page, that will be passed to a multi-modal agent along with the input text (usually gemini-2.5-pro). The agent will then review the paper and write a report about it, highlighting the good but also the bad things. The report will be placed in a file called referee.md.

The purpose of this module is to help humans review and filter papers. While some of the recommendations we have seen from executing this module are related to ways to describe and connect things, the module is also able to provide much more in-depth suggestions, such as logical flaws or underlying assumptions that invalidate reasoning or conclusions. The report generated by this module can be used to improve the quality of the generated papers via human intervention or automatic agent refinement. The prompt used for this module is found below.

- 14https://aaai.org/conference/aaai/aaai-26/keywords/
- 15https://journals.aas.org/keywords-2013/

- - Find things that may not be done correctly
