- - Check carefully that there is enough evidence in the paper to support the conclusions
- - If the results are not good, reason whether this is a surprising thing or just it used the wrong strategy and failed. If the latter, the paper should be considered bad.

Try to judge whether the paper will be worth a publication or not. Give a score from 0 (a very bad paper) to 9 (an amazing paper). For bad papers, give a low score.

**Respond in exactly this format**:

\begin{REVIEW} <REVIEW> \end{REVIEW}

In ⟨REVIEW⟩, put your report.}, { ”type”: ”image url”, ”image url”: {”url”: f”data:image/png;base64,image b64”}} for image b64 in state[’referee’][’images’]

### 4 Usage

In its current form, Denario can be run in two different ways:

- • Python API
- • Graphical User Interface (GUI)

The Python API can be run in Python scripts or Jupyter notebooks, while the GUI can be run either locally or through a web application. In the following subsections we detail the usage of each case.

##### 4.1 Python API

The main entrypoint of Denario is its Python API, which allows the user to call the different modules. For that, the user firstly needs to install the software locally. Denario is publicly available on GitHub16 and pypi,17 and can be easily installed by running the command: pip install denario. We refer the reader to the documentation18 for further details on how to install the package. A typical Python script to perform end-to-end research is this:

from denario import Denario, Journal # Initiate Denario by setting the working directory den = Denario(project_dir="project_dir") # Set the input text with data description input_text = """ Analyze the experimental data stored in /path/to/data.csv using sklearn and pandas. This data includes time-series measurements from a particle detector. """ den.set_data_description(input_text) # Generate a research idea from the input text den.get_idea() # check whether the idea is new or not den.check_idea() # Generate a research plan to carry out the idea den.get_method() # Follow the research plan, write and execute code, make plots, and summarize the results den.get_results() # Write a paper for the APS journal den.get_paper(journal=Journal.APS) # Review the paper den.referee()

###### The Python API also allows to set research idea and methods provided by the user:

# Set the idea given by a text file in the project folder den.set_idea()

# or providing an input string den.set_idea("Write a research idea here")

# Similarly, set the methods given by a text file in the project folder (or providing an input string) den.set_method()

It is possible to select between the different backends, Cmbagent and the default fast method based on LangGraph for idea and method generation:

# Generate an idea using the fast method based on the LangGraph implementation (default option) den.get_idea(mode="fast")

# Generate an idea using the Cmbagent backend den.get_idea(mode="cmbagent")

The code above can be executed in several ways. For example, the lines can be saved in a Python script and run using python script.py. Alternatively, the code can be executed interactively in environments such as a Jupyter notebook or Google Colab. For more details on the implementation and syntax of the Python API, please refer to the Denario documentation19.

- 16https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/Denario
- 17https://pypi.org/project/denario/
- 18https://denario.readthedocs.io
- 19https://denario.readthedocs.io

##### 4.2 Graphical User Interface

###### 4.2.1 Launch locally

Denario also provides a Graphical User Interface (GUI) to facilitate its usage, which is shown in Fig. 9. It can be installed from pypi with the extension pip install denario[app]. The GUI can be then launched running denario run, which will open a tab in the browser with the application. Its repository is also publicly available at GitHub20.

[Figure 8]

Figure 9: This figure shows the Graphical User Interface (GUI) of Denario. In the upper-left part, the user can set the API keys for the LLMs. Below that part, the user can upload data and download the files generated by Denario. In the central part, the user can choose which module to run and can tune the options available for it (e.g. LLM model). If the user wants to perform end-to-end research, she/he will have to run the different modules sequentially.

In the GUI, the user can set the API keys for the LLM models to use, upload the data to be analyzed and other input files, and download the files generated by Denario. The input text can be passed either by typing it directly into the GUI, or by uploading a file with the text.

The GUI includes several tabs for each of the Denario modules, where the user can choose which one to run. It is possible to provide input files too through these tabs. For instance, if the user wants to generate a research methodology, but wants to provide the idea to carry out, he/she should first select the Idea tab and upload the research idea there. Next, the user should go to the Methods tabs and run the module there. After running it, Denario will generate the research methodology that can be used for other modules, such as the analysis one. The required inputs and the outputs generated by each module can be found in Table 1.

###### 4.2.2 Web application

The GUI discussed above is meant to be used locally, e.g., on a personal computer. The advantage is that the user can leverage local resources such as a GPU or multiple CPUs, while a potential barrier is that the user needs to install Denario and its dependencies locally. To circumvent this and to provide a quick way to experiment with Denario, we also provide users with the option to run it as a web application. In this case, no installation is needed and the user can start using Denario immediately. On the other hand, the free resources available to the user (e.g., data storage, CPUs, GPUs) may be limited. We currently provide two ways to access it online:

20https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioApp

- • HuggingFace Spaces app. A demo of Denario is hosted as a web app on HuggingFace Spaces21. The interface is essentially the same as the local GUI (see Fig. 9).
- • Cloud-hosted app. Denario can also be deployed on general cloud platforms, allowing users to access and run it directly through a browser. Please refer to the Denario documentation for up-to-date details on the available deployment options.

### 5 End-to-end research examples

In this section, we illustrate the capabilities of Denario by showing and discussing multiple papers fully generated by it. To demonstrate the versatility of the system, we show papers generated on a very diverse set of disciplines, including astrophysics, biology, biophysics, biomedical informatics, chemistry, material science, mathematical physics, medicine, neuroscience, and planetary science. Furthermore, Denario can also be used for interdisciplinary research. We illustrate this by showing a paper that applies techniques from deep learning and quantum physics to cosmological data in Sec. 5.13.

Most of the generated papers have little to none human intervention in the generation process, besides providing and adjusting the input prompts and data. Some of them have been tested varying the input prompt with different levels of detail. For instance, in the paper discussed in Sec. 5.12 we showcase a human-in-the-loop example, where the prompt is iteratively improved using Cmbagent and human feedback.

In each of the subsections below, we provide details about the data used, the input text, the generated paper and briefly discuss the positive and negative aspects of the generated paper. The reader can find all generated files, plots, text, etc for all papers below and many more at the example papers repository22.

##### 5.1 Mathematical Physics. High-level analysis and abstraction of complex structures: the physics of non-linear PDEs

A central challenge of research in physics lies in interpreting complex results and reducing them to a framework from which general principles can be drawn. It is this capacity for abstraction that enables scientific advancement. The problem we posed Denario to solve is the following: we would like to understand the structure of the solutions to the Burgers equation in fluid dynamics for different values of the viscosity ν and initial conditions. In 1-dimension, the Burgers equation is:

∂2u ∂x2

∂u ∂x

∂u ∂t

+ u

= ν

(1)

###### 5.1.1 Background: PINNs

Our tool to solve the Burgers equation is a neural network algorithm called PINNs (physics-informed neural networks) in its implementation in the package neurodifeqq23. The PINN will find a space of solutions for different values of the viscosity and initial conditions. This creates a so-called latent space.

Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), first introduced in the works of Dissanayake and PhanThien [33] and Lagaris et al. [34], have emerged as a powerful tool for solving partial and ordinary differential equations (PDEs/ODEs). Raissi et al. [35] proved this approach to be valid on a wide variety of challenging physical problems, while other researchers have made significant advancements in applying neural networks to PDEs and ODEs, including notable examples such as [36, 37, 38]. In this paradigm, one typically trains a distinct neural network for each unknown function in the governing equations. The training process involves minimizing a loss function that encodes the squared residuals of these differential equations, thereby embedding the physics directly into the learning objective.

In the PINNs setup, we use one NN for every unknown function appearing in the differential equations. We call these objects ψNN(xµ) and they represent the approximate solution given by the NNs for different points along the independent variable and possibly different values of parameter or boundary conditions (all of them are represented by xµ). The training process involves minimizing the loss function, typically defined as the residuals of the differential equations squared, summed across all the sample points of the input domain:

- 21https://huggingface.co/spaces/astropilot-ai/Denario
- 22https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioExamplePapers
- 23https://github.com/NeuroDiffGym/neurodiffeq

(DψNN(xµ))2 + λLadd (2)

###### L =

batch

where D represents a differential operator that will depend on the differential equations that we are considering. Here Ladd represents any additional contribution to the loss that can be added to give extra information to the model during training. The weight of this piece is controlled by λ.

While traditional numerical methods often outperform PINNs in terms of computational efficiency and accuracy, recent developments in PINNs are offering unique advantages. One key benefit is the ability of PINNs to learn the parametric dependence of the solutions to different initial or boundary conditions, or even different values of parameters appearing in the equations. In contrast with traditional numerical methods, this allows us to train the model on a wide range of different parameters at once, whereas a traditional solver must be rerun for different values of initial/boundary conditions or parameters. This eventually will make a PINNs setup much more efficient compared with a numerical method, since obtaining a solution for a particular value of a parameter just requires the evaluation of the model. This efficient evaluation permits us to treat otherwise untreatable problems. One of which is the so-called inverse problem [39, 40]. This consists of recovering a free-form function or parameter appearing on the differential equations just by considering boundary data. This capability is extremely useful for this work, since we will use it to recover the viscosity of Burger’s equation by considering the initial and final time configuration of a solution. Another key advantage of PINNs is their capability of learning a general highdimensional space of functions called the latent space. The final solution would just be a combination of these functions in a certain way. This latent space will, in general, depend on the independent variables of the problem, but it can also be learned for more parameters, like different boundary conditions or different values of a parameter appearing in the equations. In this work, we learn a latent space of Burger’s equation for different values of the viscosity ν in the so-called Multihead training. We will explain this framework in the following subsection.

Although we have presented the two main advantages that we are going to exploit throughout this work of using PINNs instead of traditional numerical methods, there exist many more. PINNs are meshfree, allowing for obtaining a solution at any point lying inside the training set. Moreover, they can also be used to find new solutions on stiff regimes using their ability to transfer learning [40].

###### 5.1.2 Multihead training

Multihead (MH) training consists of breaking the neural network into two pieces: the body, which will learn a higher-dimensional representation (latent space) of the solutions depending on the values of different parameters or boundary conditions; and the head, which will take care of learning how to project from this latent space to the actual solution. This setup has already been proven useful to transfer learn solutions of differential equations to stiffer regimes. However, we use MH training to explore the functions of the latent space when the head is forced to present a linear response. This will tell us valuable information about the functional “basis” that the model is learning to solve the problem.

The NN gives us the final solution ψNN(xµ) composed of two parts

- • Body: this itself is going to be a NN which is going to learn a high-dimensional space called the latent

space of solutions. We will denote it as Hi(xµ), where i runs from 1 to the total dimensionality of this space. In general, this NN must be large enough such that it can learn a proper representation of the solutions in this higher-dimensional space. In general, this body will take as inputs the independent variable plus variations of parameters or different boundary conditions of the equations, denoted by xµ. After passing them through the model, it will return us the latent space Hi(xµ), which will be composed of d components.

- • Head: this component is also going to be a NN and will take care of processing the latent space component and combine them on a particular way such that the final result is going to be the desired approximate solution to the differential equation ψNN(xµ). In general, this model is much smaller than the body, since only a few operations on the latent space will be required to produce the final solution. Generally, the head will take the latent space of dimension d, and combine its components such that the final output is dimension 1. We will have one head for each of the values of the free parameter or boundary conditions that we are considering. Thus, each of them will learn a particular set of weights and biases that will project down the latent space to the solution for a particular value of the parameters and boundary conditions chosen.

At the end, the solution can be expressed as ψNN(xµ) = headW[Hi(xµ)] where head denotes the response of the head, and W the set of its weights and biases.

The model is trained as follows. Once one approximated solution is obtained, we can compute its loss function just by evaluating the residues of the differential equations squared (2). The total loss will be the sum of each of the individual losses across all the heads. We can then train the model by optimizing this loss function. At the end, the model will solve simultaneously all specified differential equations problems. It is important to note that, since the body is shared across all NNs, it will capture global properties of the solutions for different values of free parameter or boundary conditions.

###### 5.1.3 Latent space structure with Denario

Our question to Denario then was to find the structure of the latent space generated by training on Burger’s equation for different initial conditions and values of the viscosity. The reason behind it was that the structure of the latent space might reveal the actual physics determining the structure of the solutions to this equation. So we asked Denario to explore the structure of the latent space of solutions, having given it the following results: we provided an array that contained the latent space solutions as a function of ν, space, and time. The input text passed to Denario was this:

Input text

We haved PINNs to solve a Burger equation in 2 dimensions for a fixed value of the viscosity with multihead set for different initial conditions. The latent space is located in this file

/Users/fvillaescusa/Documents/Software/Denario/Project\_turbulence/data\_for\_Paco\_turbulence\ _bundle.npy

###### To read the data, you can do:

import numpy as np fin = ’/Users/fvillaescusa/Documents/Software/Denario/Project_turbulenceV1/

data_for_Paco_turbulence_bundle.npy’ data = np.load(fin)

data is now a [101,103,25,13] matrix, where the first axis represents the x-coordinate, the second axis is time, and the third component represents the viscosity. The fourth axis is organized as follows: - first three components are the mesh of space, time and the viscosity, respectively - the rest (10 last components) the latent space Perform a detailed study of the latent space structure. We are interested in knowing if there is some pattern or simple way to describe its properties.

We have run Denario end-to-end from the above prompt to generate a final article. The generated paper, titled Geometric Structure of PINN Latent Space for Burger’s Equation: Low-Dimensional Manifolds and Initial Condition Encoding, can be found in the Appendix A.1. In this paper, Denario performed a detailed analysis of the given latent space of Burger’s equation. It applied common techniques of dimensionality reduction on the provided data set, mainly Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and subspace similarity measures. Although this analysis is quite standard, it includes some points that were surprising. The first one was a detailed analysis of the centroids of the manifolds, computing their PCA individually and discovering that there was only one dominant component when varying the viscosity. Then, it performed a similar analysis on the 3-dimensional principal subspaces for each value of the viscosity. This analysis included subspace similarity between these manifolds and the dot products of these vectors. The conclusion was that these manifolds were almost parallel to each other, and that they described up to 97.67% of the variance. At last, it analyzed the global structure of the latent space using the previously mentioned techniques. It concluded that the PINN is learning a 3-dimensional manifold to describe a solution for each value of the viscosity. Variations of this parameter are encoded as translations of this 3-dimensional space across a 1-dimensional sub-manifold. We would also like to remark that Denario produced unexpected results at one point. Throughout the whole paper, it is remarked that the data is obtained for different initial conditions. However, this is not true, and the index that was treated as different initial conditions corresponded to different values of the viscosity. This confusion was due to a

misleading prompt on our side. In this respect, Denario showed robustness in that it followed the prompt instructions and did not simply try to repeat what is in the literature.

As a summary, we would like to remark on the analysis that Denario has performed on the data, not

- as a novel and groundbreaking job, but as a tool for researchers to unveil future directions that are worth investigating in detail.

##### 5.2 Planetary Science. Mapping Size and Compositional Gradients in the Asteroid Belt

The asteroid belt preserves a fossil record of the solar system’s formation and dynamical evolution. We compiled a dataset of over 35,000 main-belt asteroids, integrating orbital parameters, diameters, and spectral types. These data were obtained from a wide range of sources, including the Lowell dataset [41], the Asteroid Lightcurve Database (LCDB) [42], DAMIT [43], mp3c [44], and the Python tool classy [45]. We then asked Denario to analyze the data. The input text we used was this:

Input text

We have some data about asteroids. The data is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Asteroids/data

Each asteroid is identified by a unique number. For example, 1 corresponds to the first discovered asteroid, Ceres.

All CSV files share a common structure:

- • Column 1: Asteroid identification number
- • Column 2: Corresponding physical or orbital property

These files are recommended to be opened with the Python package ”pandas”. File Descriptions:

- • asteroid name.csv: number + name of the asteroid

- • asteroid diameter.csv: number + diameter of the asteroid in kilometers

- • asteroid semimajor axis.csv: number + semimajor axis of the orbit in astronomical units (AU)

- • asteroid eccentricity.csv: number + eccentricity of the orbit

- • asteroid inclination.csv: number + inclination of the orbit in degrees

- • asteroid arg peri.csv: number + argument of periapsis of the orbit in degrees

- • asteroid long asc node.csv: number + longitude of ascending node of the orbit in degrees

- • asteroid spin period.csv: number + spin period of the asteroid in hours

- • asteroid obliquity.csv: number + obliquity of the asteroid in degrees (Obliquity is defined as the angle between the spin vector and the orbital angular momentum vector.)

- • asteroid type.csv: number + spectral type of the asteroid

- • asteroid family.csv: number + family name of the asteroid (The family name corresponds to the largest member of the family)

- • asteroid age.csv: number + age of the asteroid in gigayears (Gyr)

Please come up with an interesting project for a PhD thesis. Use state-of-the-art methods to analyze the data. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to indicate whether the execution was successful or not. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data. You have access to 128 cpus; for computationally heavy tasks, try to use all of them.

The generated paper, titled The Spatial Architecture of the Main Asteroid Belt: Size, Composition, and Dynamical Gradients, can be found in the Appendix A.2. By applying density estimation, clustering (DBSCAN and GMM), and predictive modeling, Denario mapped spatial variations in size and composition, identified asteroid families, and examined the influence of Jupiter’s resonances on the belt’s structure. A particular strength of the paper lies in its ability to automate the quantification of compositional gradients across the belt. This paper reveals an important compositional trend: the dominant composition shifts from S-type in the inner solar system to C-type in the outer solar system. By mapping the changing fractions of spectral types as a function of semimajor axis, it offers an accessible, up-to-date reference that will be useful for researchers studying planetesimal formation and solar system evolution. The clustering analyses also effectively reproduce known asteroid families, confirming the AI’s capacity to extract meaningful dynamical structures from complex data.

However, while these results are scientifically sound, they are not fundamentally new. The compositional gradient and dynamical families are well-established in the literature. The observed trend of increasing average asteroid size with distance from the Sun is also correctly noted as likely driven by observational bias rather than a genuine physical gradient. One area for improvement is the depth of interpretation. While Denario correctly applied clustering and density estimation, it stops at describing known structures without critically assessing the potential for new dynamical groupings that might hint

- at unrecognized collisional families or early migration signatures. This illustrates a broader limitation: although AI can uncover patterns efficiently, it currently lacks the domain intuition to pose new hypotheses or recognize subtle, novel features without human input.

Similarly, the paper’s predictive modeling using only orbital data yielded limited success, appropriately acknowledging the role of stochastic collisional histories. But it could have gone further by discussing how including additional parameters—such as albedo, spin state, or detailed spectral data—might improve model performance. On the other hand, in its current form, Denario is not designed to do this kind of critical thinking, so perhaps it is not a surprise that it does not perform well here.

It is also worth noting the experience with another AI-generated paper (not included here, but available in the example papers repository24), which focused on spin-orbit coupling effects. In that case, Denario produced a figure that appeared to show features not previously discussed in the literature. However, Denario itself did not recognize or highlight these potentially novel patterns, and other figures in that paper were poorly prepared, limiting its usefulness. This example underscores both the promise and the current limitations of AI approaches: when handling large, complex datasets, AI can be more efficient than humans at surfacing candidate phenomena, but human expertise is essential to interpret, validate, and refine these discoveries. With careful collaboration, such human–AI iteration could focus attention on these features in subsequent analyses, potentially leading to truly novel scientific breakthroughs.

Overall, while this paper does not claim any fundamentally new discovery, that is not a significant flaw. It demonstrates that Denario can systematically confirm and clearly document established knowledge, producing scientifically valuable and well-visualized results in an efficient, reproducible manner. As the era of big data arrives with observatories like Very Large Telescope (VLT) [46], the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) [47], and The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) [48], tools like Denario will become indispensable in planetary and exoplanetary science—helping researchers sift massive datasets, probe early solar system conditions, and advance our understanding of the origins of life both here and beyond.

##### 5.3 Medicine and Health Services Research. Assessment of Fertility Clinic Outcomes in the United States

Health services research is a multidisciplinary field that studies healthcare utilization, access, delivery, and financing, with the goal of improving the quality, efficiency, and equity of healthcare. Combining insights from medicine, public health, economics, and statistics, health services research aims to inform decisions by providers, payers, policymakers, and patients.

To evaluate Denario’s capability to design and perform a project in this field, we used the publicly available datasets from the National ART Surveillance System25. These annual datasets, published in the United States by the CDC (US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), contain clinic-level aggregated data on the utilization and success rates of approximately 98% of all assisted reproductive technology (ART) services in the United States. Originally mandated by the US Congress to provide transparency and information to patients seeking fertility treatments, these datasets have been extensively used to evaluate the quality, efficiency, and distribution of fertility services.

- 24https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioExamplePapers
- 25https://www.cdc.gov/art/php/nass

More specifically, we provided Denario with the three most recent years available for NASS (20202022) and a description of the dataset and its variables. We then instructed Denario to suggest and develop potentially interesting venues of scientific investigation. The exact input text we provided it with is this:

Input text

The Final Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) Success Rates dataset is part of the CDC’s National ART Surveillance System (NASS) and provides clinic-level success rate data for procedures conducted between 2020 and 2022. It includes information from U.S. fertility clinics on ART cycles, distinguishing whether patients used their own eggs or donor eggs, and whether ART was their first treatment or a follow-up. The dataset presents cumulative success rates (including embryo transfers over 12 months after retrieval) for own-egg patients by retrieval and transfer, and non-cumulative rates for donor-egg cycles. It also includes statistics like average transfers per retrieval and retrievals per live birth. These data—updated most recently in December 2024 and made public in early 2025—offer insights into clinic performance and national ART outcomes. Among the dataset’s relevant columns are:

- • ClinicID – unique identifier linking this Success Rates dataset to other ART data (Services, Characteristics, Summary).
- • Reporting Year – the calendar year.
- • Age Group – patient age brackets (e.g., <35, 35–37, 38–40, etc.).
- • Live Birth per Intended Retrieval – percentage of intended egg retrieval cycles resulting in live births within a year.
- • Live Birth per Transfer – percentage of embryo transfer cycles resulting in live births within the same reporting window.
- • Live Birth per Actual Retrieval – reflecting actual retrieval procedures conducted.
- • Avg Transfers per Intended Retrieval – average number of embryo transfers per intended retrieval.
- • Avg Intended Retrievals per Live-Birth – average number of retrieval cycles needed to yield a live birth.
- • Donor Egg Live Birth Rate – percentage of donor-egg embryo transfer cycles leading to live births.
- • Clinic Export Variables – additional metrics such as clinic location, number of cycles, and whether it was first-time ART cycles.

These columns capture both performance and efficiency metrics, enabling comparisons across clinics and patient groups—own-egg vs. donor-egg, first-time vs. any-time ART, age categories, and aggregated national data. The description of the columns, together with their data type is this:

The generated paper, titled Characterizing the Variability and Correlates of U.S. ART Clinic Performance During the COVID-19 Pandemic (2020-2022), can be found in the Appendix A.3. In this paper, Denario characterized the year-to-year variability in success and efficiency metrics of ART clinics, such as live birth rates per retrieval and average retrievals per live birth, stratified by patient age and egg source (own vs. donor). The dataset was evaluated using standard statistical analyses, such as the coefficient of variation, to analyze fluctuations in success rates, ordinary least squares regression models, and Spearman correlation to characterize associations between variability and clinic volume. While the analyses were relatively straightforward and would likely need to be redone using other statistical tools, the contextualization and characterization of the research question were remarkable. Despite the recognized importance of inter-clinic variability in outcomes, little attention has been given to the characterization of year-to-year intra-clinic fluctuations in ART clinic performance, particularly in the context of a major systemic shock like the COVID-19 pandemic. Denario contextualized the research by not only evaluating an overlooked topic in the literature, but also by realizing the impact of the global pandemic on healthcare systems through disruptions like clinic closures, supply chain issues, and shifts in patient behavior.

The final manuscript generated by Denario had some limitations on the presentation of the results and in the citations to the literature. The results and overall content of the manuscript were significantly more technical than the standard in the field, which generally focuses more on the discussion and implications of the results. Statistical analyses were limited to standard tools such as ordinary least squares and correlations, which (as recognized in the manuscript) would need to be re-evaluated given

the distributional properties of the variability measures. Another limitation was the fact that Denario used only open-access manuscripts available at preprint repositories, such as the arXiv. While the use of preprint repositories is a common practice in most technical areas, including economics, their use is still limited in the field of health services research and most areas of medicine. For this reason, the references included in the final manuscript generated by Denario were not necessarily applicable and were, at best, marginally relevant to the sentence in which they are used.

Nonetheless, despite the limitations described above, the research conducted by Denario was genuinely engaging and interesting, highlighting an understudied topic in the area and contextualizing it in a novel way. This manuscript not only identifies promising directions for future investigation but also includes methodology and results that would be useful resources for researchers in the field to further their investigations.

##### 5.4 Chemistry. Molecular dynamics simulations of self-assembling peptides

Self-assembling peptides (SAPs) are promising candidates for biomedical applications such as tissue engineering, wound healing, and drug delivery. Their modular structure and biocompatibility make them especially attractive for engineering soft materials with targeted functions. Understanding the relationship between structure and properties in SAPs is key to unlocking this potential. To investigate this, we tasked Denario with analyzing a 1200 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) trajectory containing 30 copies of a known self-assembling pentapeptide: KYFIL. We conducted the study over three rounds26, each time increasing the level of contextual information provided in the input text.

In the first round, we instructed Denario on which Python tools to use for trajectory analysis but gave no domain-specific context. Denario correctly identified the system as a protein but misinterpreted it as a single large molecule rather than 30 individual peptides. As a result, it analyzed residues in isolation, failing to recognize that they were equivalent across different peptide chains. This led to an overemphasis on per-residue metrics like dihedral angles or motif detection, rather than ensemble behaviors across peptides. Consequently, key phenomena like peptide aggregation and clustering were missed.

In the second round, we added a system description and a research abstract to provide context. With this information, Denario identified more appropriate analyses related to self-assembly, such as contact mapping and cluster size distributions. While the outputs were more relevant, they remained conventional and did not go beyond standard MD analysis pipelines. However, the automation of routine essential tasks was already a valuable outcome.

In the third round, we explicitly posed hypotheses and research questions. Specifically, we suggested modeling peptide clusters as graphs and proposed several graph-theoretical analyses, along with practical motivations for each. The input text we used for this round is this:

Input text

We have data from a molecular dynamics numerical simulation. The data is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Project chemist1/data. This trajectory contains an all atom molecular dynamics simulation of 30 copies of the self-assembling pentapeptide, K-Y-F-I-L. The simulation starts with the peptides fully separated and over the course of the simulation the peptides form noncovalent interactions with one another to form an aggregate.

Motivation: The development of biomaterials that mimic the native extracellular matrix (ECM) of brain tissue represents a promising frontier for neural repair and regeneration. Injectable hydrogels made of short, self-assembling peptides offer a promising platform for the delivery and directed differentiation of therapeutic stem cells. Despite the growing interest in this field, the rational design of self-assembling peptide sequences remains largely empirical. Our research aims to address this gap by computationally modeling a library of rapidly assembling pentapeptides for injectable delivery (RAPID)-a family of C-terminally amidated, five-residue peptides engineered to self-assemble into shear-thinning, self-healing hydrogels. These RAPID hydrogels have demonstrated the potential to improve cell survival upon minimally invasive delivery. To better understand the mechanisms behind assembly behavior, we examined KYFIL, a pentapeptide known to self-assemble, using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to determine the molecular scale behaviors that distinguish gelling from non-gelling sequences.

26In other words, we generated papers from slightly different prompts.

The folder contains two files:

- 1. stripped.nc: the trajectory file which contains the coordinates as a function of time
- 2. stripped.parm7: contains information about what each of the atom types are (which coordinates belong to which molecules).

The data can be read as:

import MDAnalysis as mda # Load the AMBER topology and trajectory topology_file = ’system.prmtop’ # Replace with your actual .prmtop file trajectory_file = ’trajectory.nc’ # Replace with your actual trajectory file # Create the Universe object u = mda.Universe(topology_file, trajectory_file) # Print some basic info print("Number of atoms:", len(u.atoms)) print("Number of frames in trajectory:", len(u.trajectory)) # Accessing trajectory frames for ts in u.trajectory[:5]: # Iterate through the first 5 frames

print(f"Frame: {ts.frame}, Time: {ts.time} ps")

###### Considerations:

- • In order to understand how the simulated system compares to experiments, we need to understand how the system behaves at equilibrium (or as close to equilibrium as possible). Therefore, we are most interested in measuring quantities starting from about 100ns into the trajectory until the end of the trajectory (as opposed to the beginning of the trajectory).
- • We are interested in making graphs that are either a function of time or averaged over long time intervals. We are not interested in measurements that are averaged over small time intervals or representative of a single snapshot.

###### Research Questions:

- • You can consider the peptides aggregates as two different types of graphs:

- – First, a graph where each peptides is a node and an edge between nodes represents the binary property of whether or not those two nodes have a heavy atom contact
- – Second, where the aggregates are a hierarchical graph, where the coarse grained graph is the same as above, but each peptide is additionally made up of a fine grained graph where every amino acid is a node

- • With these two graph definitions we can measure graph theoretical properties, which tell us about the overall structure of the graph

- – We can construct the graph laplacian and calculate eigenvectors and eigenvalues
- – We can calculate the Fiedler vector
- – Are there other interesting graph theoretical quantities to explore?

- • We would want to know how do these properties:

- – Look on average?
- – Fluctuate about that average?
- – Change dynamically over time?

- • We would like these properties to tell us:

- – How densely packed are the clusters?
- – Can this approach be used to predict whether a cluster will split or be long lived?

- – What are different ways that we can measure peptide clusters or aggregates?

∗ Our current definition is that a cluster is a set of nodes where none of the nodes is fully disconnected from any of the other nodes. But one challenge with this is that the number of clusters varies widely as clusters form and uniform over the simulation. Is there a way to combine this measurement with some graph theoretical definition of graph density in order to construct a more stable order parameter?

Use state-of-the-art methods to analyze the data. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to indicate whether the execution was successful or not. Take into account that all the things print on screen will be passed to a LLM, thus, only write essential information and don’t print unnecessary information. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data. You have access to 128 cpus on a linux machine; for very computationally heavy tasks, try to use all of them.

With this guidance, Denario performed novel, domain-relevant analyses that had not been previously utilized in the field of peptide self-assembly—and executed them efficiently. The generated paper, titled Dynamic Multiscale Graph Analysis Reveals Structural Signatures of Peptide Aggregate Stability and Splitting can be found in the Appendix A.4. These results showed that, for Denario to exhibits its full capability, a very detailed and extensive description of the data is needed, and in some cases, guidance over the research direction.

Overall, Denario demonstrated a clear progression in capability based on the depth of contextual input. With minimal context, it could automate standard analyses; with targeted hypotheses, it extended into novel analytical territory. While Denario didn’t independently generate insights a human expert wouldn’t have, it significantly accelerated the exploration of both standard and creative research avenues.

##### 5.5 Astrophysics. Properties of recent high-mass binary black hole merger from gravitational wave data

We provided Denario with publicly available gravitational wave posteriors [49] from multiple waveform models for a recently announced gravitational wave event GW231123 [50]. GW231123 is the most massive confident black hole merger detected till now and has implications for the formation channels of astrophysical black holes. However, there is a significant disagreement between properties of the event as predicted by different waveform models (see their description in the prompt below). This was the motivation for us to perform an exploratory study with Denario regarding the high-dimensional posterior dataset from multiple models.

The input text we used for this paper is this: Input text We have data from a recent gravitational wave event: GW231123. The data is located in five files:

- - /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/GW/Iteration1/data/GW231123\_NRSur7dq4.csv

- - /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/GW/Iteration1/data/GW231123\_IMRPhenomXO4a.csv

- - /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/GW/Iteration1/data/GW231123\_SEOBNRv5PHM.csv

- - /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/GW/Iteration1/data/GW231123\_IMRPhenomXPHM.csv

- - /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/GW/Iteration1/data/GW231123\_IMRPhenomTPHM.csv

These files contain samples from the posterior distribution corresponding to five different gravitational-wave waveform models which are detailed below. The meaning of each column can be found in the file header, but is also provided below for reference.

We are interested in understanding which ways the different models agree or differ in their prediction for GW231123. There are complex degeneracies in the high-dimensional posterior space which make this problem challenging. Analyze the datasets in detail and tell us what you have learned from them. Mention also any interesting astrophysical insights that you learn from this analysis, and what can be robustly concluded about statistical properties of the high-mass black hole merger GW231123. Make sure there is no repetition in plots in the paper. For reference, the event was reported in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.08219

Below is a description of the models used for the five files mentioned above:

- • NRSur7dq4 is a time-domain waveform model that has been directly calibrated using Numerical Relativity simulations of binary black hole mergers. This model is particularly wellsuited for events with short gravitational wave signals, such as GW231123, as it is designed to accurately capture the dynamics of the late inspiral, merger, and ringdown phases.
- • IMRPhenomXO4a, on the other hand, is a phenomenological model that operates in the frequency domain. It combines post-Newtonian (PN) approximations during the inspiral phase with a numerical relativity calibration near the merger. This model provides a more global approximation of binary black hole waveforms and is specifically tailored for events that can be characterized over a wider range of frequencies.
- • SEOBNRv5PHM Domain: Time-domain, effective-one-body (EOB) Form: Co-precessing to inertial frame Key: Efficient inspiral-merger-ringdown with higher modes Calibrated to: NR

+ perturbation theory, high accuracy (unfaithfulness < 3% in 99.8% of cases)

- • IMRPhenomXPHM Domain: Frequency-domain, phenomenological Form: ”Twisting-up” non-precessing multipoles into precessing frame Key: Multipolar, fast, calibrated to waveform catalogs
- • IMRPhenomTPHM Domain: Time-domain, phenomenological Form: Time-based twistingup using Euler angles + improved ringdown precession treatment Key: Avoids stationary phase, accurate and computationally efficient

Here is a description of the columns in the csv file:

- • ‘mass 1 source’: Mass of the primary black hole

- • ‘mass 2 source’: Mass of the secondary black hole

- • ‘a 1’: Spin magnitude of the primary black hole

- • ‘a 2’: Spin magnitude of the secondary black hole

- • ‘final mass source’: Final mass the remnant black hole

- • ‘final spin’: Final spin of the remnant black hole

- • ‘redshift’: Redshift of the event
- • ‘cos tilt 1’: Cosine of the spin tilt-angle of the primary black hole

- • ‘cos tilt 2’: Cosine of the spin tilt-angle of the secondary black hole

- • ‘chi eff’: Effective sum of spins components aligned with the orbital angular momentum

- • ‘chi p’: Effective spin parameter related to spin-orbit precession of the binary

- • ‘cos theta jn’: Cosine of the inclination angle of the binary to the observer

- • ‘phi jl’: Azimuthal angle between the total and orbital angular momentum (called spin azimuth)

- • ‘log likelihood’: Log-likelihood of the samples

Use state-of-the-art methods to analyze the data. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to indicate whether the execution was successful or not. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data.

The generated paper, titled Physics-Informed Discrepancy Decomposition and Robust Astrophysical Inference for GW231123, can be found in the Appendix A.5. In this paper, Denario performed the exploratory data analysis very well. Without an explicit mention of which tool(s) would be the best to

use, Denario identified dimensionality reduction tools like UMAP (which have not been widely used in the previous gravitational wave literature) for this problem. The resulting 2D UMAP embeddings in Fig. 2 of the paper have a very interesting structure. The different waveform models are built in either the time or frequency domain. The UMAP embeddings produce a common cluster for the three timedomain models, suggesting that their predicted posteriors are consistent with each other. However, for the two frequency domain models, the embeddings form separate isolated groups, highlighting that their predictions are inconsistent with each other (Fig. 2). Denario also verified that the physical explanations are independent of the hyperparameters (see Fig. 3). The Jensen-Shannon divergence plots in Fig. 4 are useful for getting an intuition of which parameters the different models differ.

This paper can be comparable to a report generated from an undergraduate-level data exploration project. While the paper is not currently ready to be published in a scientific journal, it definitely provides interesting ideas for further exploration (it can be turned into a scientific paper upon further refinement of some of the ideas presented). With each paper taking a very small time to generate, speed definitely is the biggest advantage of using Denario and it can be used to obtain quick project ideas from a dataset. The drawback is Denario not having knowledge of the broader context of the field (apart from the information specified in the prompt, and to some extent the summaries provided by the ‘enhanced data’, and ‘check idea’ options). Thus, it could not fully place the methods and results of the paper within the context of existing literature (which is crucial for a research paper). However, one can envision further developing our literature agents so they can perform these tasks using tools such as Semantic Scholar.

##### 5.6 Astrophysics. Impact of Convection and Radiation Pressure on the Dynamics of Roche Lobe Overflow in Binary Systems

Massive stars play many important roles in astrophysics. However, the structures and evolutions of massive stars remain very uncertain due to complicated dynamical processes controlled by both gas pressure and radiation pressure. In particular, the majority of massive stars are found in binary systems. Interactions with the companion can significantly impact the evolution of massive stars. Binary interactions and the associated mass transfer via the Roche Lobe overflow are the physical origins of many astrophysical phenomena. In recent years, with the advanced computational power and improved numerical algorithms, it is now possible to simulate the process of binary mass transfer between massive stars using three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations.

One simulation we have analyzed is a binary system with a 12 solar mass Red supergiant (RSG) star as a donor and a 9 solar mass main-sequence star as an accretor. The simulation resolved the threedimensional structures at the surface of the donor and followed the mass transfer to the accretor due to the binary interaction. The surface of RSG is fully convective, which can make the Roche Lobe overflow significantly different from what has been imagined in classical theoretical models. We used Denario to analyze one snapshot of the simulation results to understand how the binary mass transfer happened in the simulation. The prompt we used as input to Denario is this:

Input text

We have a snapshot of a simulation designed to study the impact of realistic 3D envelope structures on the mass transfer in a binary system. The binary is made of a 12.9 solar mass red supergiant (RSG) and a 9 solar mass companion. The companion is located at a separation of 2000 solar radii, which is about three times the radius of the donor (the RSG). The simulation shows that the convective surface structures significantly modify the mass transfer rate in the binary system. The snapshot is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/YanFei/data/star.out1.16543.athdf

To load the data use this example:
