The paper generated by Denario, titled Convection, Radiation, and the Instantaneous Mass Transfer in Red Supergiant Binaries: A 3D Simulation Analysis, can be found in the Appendix A.6. In that paper, Denario performed a detailed analysis of different components of forces that are responsible for binary mass transfer in three-dimensional radiation hydrodynamic simulations. The paper also accurately captured the importance of convection for the properties of Roche Lobe overflow. The paper shows particular strength in quantitative analysis of the data based on the equations solved in the simulation, in a similar way that scientists will do to understand the results. Furthermore, Denario analyzed the streamlines of the flow very efficiently, which is typically much harder to do in traditional analysis. We note that for this particular paper, one of the plots generated (Figure 8) by Denario was blank, so we looked at the source code and made a tiny modification to produce the intended plot.

In the associated GitHub example papers repository27, we show examples of other papers written by Denario with the same prompt. One common weak point of these papers is that the analysis cannot be connected to the literature of binary evolution for astrophysical implications of these results. This requires some knowledge of how binary evolution is typically done in the literature and the unique advantages of these simulations, which cannot be learned from the simulation data itself. It will be interesting to see if this point can be improved by adding more guidance towards this direction in the input prompt, or by using tailored agents dedicated to these domain-specific tasks.

##### 5.7 Biology. Analyzing single-celled RNA sequencing data across the malaria parasite life cycle

Biological research has become increasingly entwined with computational analysis over the past two decades. The advent of high-throughput genetic sequencing has generated a wealth of data at a scale the field had not seen in the past. The realization that variability at the individual cell level had crucial consequences for population-level behaviors led to the development of methods for single-celled data generation, increasing the scale of datasets even further. With such massive amounts of information, computational analysis (and reanalysis) of publicly available data has become a valuable part of biological research. This presents an opportunity for AI multi-agent tools such as Denario to easily explore vast datasets, identify phenomena that would otherwise be difficult to spot, and rapidly test these lines of inquiry.

Here, we used Denario to analyze a publicly available dataset of gene expression in malaria parasite cells at different life stages. Malaria, caused by unicellular parasites of the genus Plasmodium, remains a global public health threat, causing more than 600,000 deaths in the poorest communities around the world every year, and progress in its control has stalled or reversed over the past decade [51]. Understanding the biology of Plasmodium falciparum parasites, responsible for the most lethal forms of the disease, can be critical to the development of new treatments. Many aspects of Plasmodium biology are still poorly understood due to the parasite’s evolutionary divergence from other well-known model organisms. AI multi-agent systems such as Denario could be used to help address this gap in knowledge.

27https://github.com/AstroPilot-AI/DenarioExamplePapers

We used Denario to analyze a single-celled RNA sequencing (ssRNA-seq) dataset describing gene expression (transcription) in both laboratory and field-derived strains of Plasmodium falciparum. The dataset is publicly available through the Wellcome Trust’s Malaria Cell Atlas project [52] and was previously published and analyzed by Dogga, Rop, Cudini, et al. [53].

###### 5.7.1 Input data

To allow Denario to work with the dataset, we provided two input files containing the gene expression data and metadata (“pf-ch10x-set4-ch10x-exp.csv” and “pf-ch10x-set4-ch10x-data.csv”, respectively, available in dataset “P. falciparum 10x Integrated lab strains and four natural infections” on https://www.malariacellatlas.org/data-sets/). We also provided an input text prompt describing the dataset’s origin, content, and organization. We also provided information about potentially interesting research questions to follow, including both lines of inquiry explored in the original publication by Dogga, Rop, Cudini, et al. [53] and different sets of questions not explored in the publication. However, we also explicitly left an open door for analyses not mentioned in the prompt. The prompt read as follows:

Input text

We have a collection of malaria parasite single cell transcriptomic data obtained from the Malaria Cell Atlas project and previously analyzed by Dogga et al. 2024 (paper found at doi.org/10.1126/science.adj4088). Malaria parasites have a complex life cycle in which cells transition across multiple life stages in both humans and Anopheles mosquitoes. The data collected here was obtained from malaria parasites of the species Plasmodium falciparum that were either growing in human blood culture in a laboratory setting or recovered from the blood of four asymptomatic patients from Mali. This means that the parasites are all either in the asexual intraerythrocytic development cycle or the sexual blood stages. None of them are in mosquito life stages. The data is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Biology/data

The data is presented across two different files:

The first file, “gene expression.csv”, is a 2-D matrix in which columns correspond to individual cells analyzed in the experiment and rows correspond to individual genes. The first row contains unique ID codes identifying each individual cell, while the first column contains unique codes corresponding to P. falciparum strain 3D7 gene ID codes. The entries in the matrix contain the corresponding gene’s normalized expression value within the corresponding cell.

The second file, “labels.csv”, contains a table with information about each individual cell. The column marked “CELL ID” contains the same cell ID code from the previous file. There are additional columns describing the life cycle stage, parasite strain, source (“lab” for laboratory strains; “MSC1”, “MSC3”, “MSC13”, and “MSC14” for the four patients), and days in culture (only applicable for the lab strains, not for the four patient strains which are marked as “Field” for field isolates).

There are many interesting things to uncover in the dataset. One set of questions relates to potential differences between lab strains and field isolates. Another set of questions relates to gene expression differences throughout the parasite life cycle, including key marker genes of different stages and determinants of future developmental trajectories.

I am particularly curious about uncovering potential transcription factors or other master regulators of cell cycle transitions. I suspect they might be genes that maintain low expression levels throughout the life cycle, but have increases in expression immediately prior to an increase in expression across multiple other genes denoting a change in life stage. The increase in expression of a possible transcription factor or other regulator gene would be relative to its own expression level, but would probably not achieve a particularly high expression when compared to other genes.

###### 5.7.2 Description of research output

With this information, Denario produced four different manuscripts analyzing the given data. One of them, titled Single-Cell Analysis Reveals Profound Divergence in Transcriptional Regulatory Programs Between Laboratory and Field Isolates of Plasmodium falciparum can be found in the Appendix A.7.

All four manuscripts were methodologically similar, carrying out standard practice workflows used in scRNA-seq analysis: data preprocessing, dimensionality reduction by Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) [54], clustering, trajectory inference, and pseudotime assignment using common analysis packages in Python such as SCANPY [55] (3 manuscripts) or in R such as Monocle 3 [56] (1 manuscript). All manuscripts attempted different strategies to identify regulators of gene expression and to compare the gene expression profiles of laboratory and field-derived parasites, both of which the prompt listed as a topics of particular interest. To identify regulator genes, strategies tested involved combinations of screening for low expression genes, peak/burst detection in transcription, clustering into transcriptional modules characterized by gene ontology (GO) analysis, partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [57], regression models, and reportedly consulting existing information about gene function consulted from the literature and the online database PlasmoDB, part of VEuPathDB [58, 59] (however, doing so at the time the analysis was done involved web access and a personal account; it is unclear whether Denario would be able to consult PlasmoDB at all). To examine differences in gene expression between lab and field parasites, the manuscripts compared results from the techniques listed previously, occasionally complemented by differential gene expression (DGE) analysis using the tradeSeq package (2 manuscripts) [60].

###### 5.7.3 Assessment of research output

We identified a series of notable strengths and weaknesses in the research papers generated by Denario for this project:

###### Strengths:

- • Knowledge of and engagement with established biology: As expected, Denario exhibits expert-level background knowledge on P. falciparum biology. All manuscripts discuss the complexities of the malaria parasite life cycle, correctly using specific terminology to do so despite no such information being included in the prompt. The texts are able to justify the purpose of the study being done in the context of the state of the field of malaria cell biology and the advantages of scRNA-seq with respect to previous bulk RNA-seq methods. Some manuscripts even make good use of specific knowledge of individual genes for use as positive controls validating stage transitions throughout the life cycle.
- • Proficiency with standard analysis methods: The basic pipeline used to analyze the data provided contained all the necessary steps to carry out the analysis correctly, from data pre-processing and quality control (some of which had already been done beforehand on the publicly-available dataset and was therefore redundant) through to dimensionality reduction and visualization, as explained above. The tools used were well-suited for the job, conforming to standard practices in the field.
- • Consistency with existing science: Many of the general results obtained recapitulate known science. The manuscripts were all able to successfully reconstruct the Plasmodium intraerythrocytic development cycle (IDC) from transcriptomic data. They described differences between the lab and field-derived parasite samples and even provide plausible explanations for these differences in cell type and data quality.
- • Speed: Needless to say, the speed at which entire analysis pipelines are created and the results are analyzed is far greater than what a human researcher would take. In less than a day, Denario produced analyses and manuscripts that would take multiple days or weeks, depending on a researcher’s familiarity with the methods.
- • Methodological creativity when approaching new research questions: When prompted with a research question with no clear answer nor a well-established, standardized way to address it, Denario showed remarkable creativity. All four manuscripts had different approaches for trying to identify regulator genes, as explained above.

###### Weaknesses:

- • Poor citation, acknowledgment, and engagement with existing literature: The most immediately evident shortcoming these manuscripts had was in their handling of scientific literature. Although (to the best of our knowledge) all the references cited in these manuscripts corresponded to real articles, the criteria used for selecting studies as references for specific passages is unclear. While the literature cited is related to the topic in question, it often is a perspective or review article with only general-level relevance, while highly relevant and closely related articles are left undiscussed. As an example, none of the manuscripts referenced the study by Dogga, Rop, Cudini et al. [53] describing the dataset used and its original analysis, despite this information being explicitly provided in the input prompt. Interestingly, the problem of missing citations is particularly noticeable when discussing specific facts about malaria biology, most of which are not cited at all. Indeed, only 2 out of 30 references in the manuscript shown in the supplementary material refer to malaria or Plasmodium parasites, while the other 28 refer to scRNA-seq methods. This is curious given the stark contrast with the impressive grasp of malaria parasite biology shown in the writing: Denario clearly knows the field of malaria well, but prefers to cite other fields. Perhaps Denario is more likely to include references related to the methods it uses more than the knowledge of the field it applies them to, although even references to the exact methods being used are rare. Relatedly, perhaps the lack of malaria citations and tendency to reference methods is a reflection of training biases in the quantity or perceived impact of publications in different fields: methods are generally applicable to multiple research areas and are therefore more widely cited and discussed in the literature than papers addressing a specific field such as malaria biology. This would have important ramifications that would be crucial to address in any research AI agent.
- • Confirmation bias, misplaced confidence, and overstated tone: Perhaps the most concerning weakness shown in these manuscripts is their tendency to overstate the findings they present, particularly in regard to the open-ended research question posed in the prompt regarding potential regulators of gene expression. Although all manuscripts tried a variety of creative and potentially successful strategies for identifying candidate genes involved in life cycle regulation, none of the results presented inspire great confidence. The magnitude and timing of the changes in gene expression on which the conclusions are based is not sufficient to uphold the claims made about the regulative roles of specific genes, particularly in view of the variance in gene expression. In fact, it may be the case that the signal-to-noise ratio in scRNA-seq measurements of transcription factor expression is too low to be able to draw meaningful conclusions, or that key changes in regulator activity might be occurring at a post-transcriptional level. The research question was intended to be challenging, and like any real research question, it might not have a clear answer with the available data, in which case a negative result must be reported (or at least, a lack of confidence in the results must be conveyed). It is possible that the confirmation bias shown when attempting to answer a specific research question from the prompt is a consequence of the bias against publishing negative results already found in existing scientific literature, which would skew the training dataset of any AI agents such as Denario. To be able to succeed, AI multi-agents must be able to temper their conclusions when confidence in the significance of the results is low.
- • Occasional mistaken knowledge: Although the manuscripts show a strong understanding of Plasmodium biology for the most part, occasional mistakes are made. For instance, the manuscript included as an example in the supplementary material claims that the gene Pfs25 (PF3D7 1031000) is “the canonical male gametocyte surface protein gene”, when in fact it has been repeatedly shown to be expressed solely in female gametocytes, not male ones [61]. Although not widespread throughout the manuscripts (and certainly not unique to AI agent writing when compared to human writing), the issue is complicated by the previously discussed lack of citations. Without references to the sources of information, it becomes difficult to fact-check every statement and understand why the few mistakes that occur are happening.

- • Methodological ambiguity: At multiple points in the Methods sections of different manuscripts, the text describes multiple valid but mutually exclusive methods for analysis without specifying which one was actually used (“Data loading was performed [...] in Python or R”, “Trajectories were reconstructed [...] using [...] Monocle 3, Slingshot, or PAGA”). This poses a problem when evaluating the adequacy of the work being presented, since it is not clear what the exact methodology followed was.
- • Occasional missing tables and references: The manuscript included in the supplement references tables not included in the text, although these results are calculated in the analysis code generated.

Some citations are also presumably missing, included as question marks in the text.

Overall, the application of Denario to biological datasets such as this one yields results that are impressive in their speed and competent grasp of a field and its methods, but concerning in their presentation and interpretation, as well as in the way they are presented in relation to other studies. The implications of these trends are discussed in a later section. As AI agents such as Denario continue to improve, we expect them to become transformational tools for training and research in biological sciences.

##### 5.8 Digital Health. Developing and evaluating step-counting algorithms from wrist- and hip-worn accelerometers

Wearable monitoring is a popular, emerging research field within the digital health domain, for the objective, passive monitoring of biosignals, which may offer insights into health outcomes [62]. This field has particularly grown with the increased use of smart devices such as phones and watches [63, 64]. These devices use a variety of sensors to extract digital measures, such as total sleep time, sleep efficiency, heart rate, and daily step count, among others [65]. Of these measures, the daily step count, particularly achieving 10,000 steps a day, has become one of the hallmark approaches to monitoring one’s activity levels. However, this measure still has a high degree of skepticism, due to a lack of transparency of many step counting algorithms, and known tricks to trigger false counting of steps, through arm movements [66, 67].

In this study, Denario was used to read, process, and investigate research questions using a publicly available accelerometer dataset. This data contains raw wrist and hip accelerometer data from 39 Oxfordbased participants over 1 hour. The raw data was collected from 2 devices at each location, set to sampling frequencies of 25 and 100Hz; therefore, four monitoring devices in total. A hip-mounted, foot-facing camera was used to record the timings of each step taken by participants, allowing for the annotation of an indication of the timing of each heel strike, corresponding to each step. The dataset is explained in further detail in the published work of Small et al. (2024) [67]. This dataset could primarily be used to train or validate models/algorithms used to count steps. Moreover, given the data collection from four different devices, it is possible to compare how the performance of these step-counting algorithms differs between the wrist and the hip, and at different sampling frequencies. Using the metadata file, we can further explore if there are noted differences in different age groups or sexes, though limited to just 39 participants [67].

###### 5.8.1 Input data

The full contents of the OxWalk dataset were provided to Denario. This included the raw accelerometer files, kept in separate folders for device location and sampling frequency combination. These files were stored as CSV files, with one file per participant in each folder. Within the CSV file, there are 5 columns of data. The first column is the data timestamp, and the next 3 are the accelerometer signal in x, y and z (measured in units of gravity = 9.81ms−2). The final column is an indicator of whether the heel strike of a step occurred at that time, that is, the start of a step. In addition to this, there was a single metadata CSV file, storing the age band and sex of each of the participants. After an initial attempt, we provided the following refined prompt to the Denario model:

Input text OxWalk Annotated Step Count Dataset DATA DESCRIPTION: Annotated step data during unscripted, free living in 39 healthy adult volunteers (aged 18 and above) with no lower limb injury within the previous 6 months and who were able to walk without an assistive device. Participants wore four triaxial accelerometers concurrently (AX3, Axivity, Newcastle, UK), two placed side-by-side on the dominant wrist and two clipped to the dominant-side hip at the midsagittal plane. Accelerometers were synchronised using the Open Movement GUI software (v.1.0.0.42), with one recording at 100 Hz and the other at 25 Hz at each body location. Foot-facing video was captured using an action camera (Action Camera CT9500, Crosstour, Shenzhen, China) mounted at the participant’s beltline.

DATA ANNOTATION: Foot-facing video was captured for up to one hour using an action camera (Action Camera CT9500, Crosstour, Shenzhen, China) mounted at the participant’s beltline. Annotation of steps was conducted within video annotation software (Elan 6.0, The Language Archive, Nijmegen, Netherlands), where a step was defined as the act of purposeful lifting a foot and placing it in a new location. Steps were not required to be part of a repeating pattern and did not include foot shuffling, changing of foot alignment via pivoting, or shifting of weight from one foot to the other.

DATASETS: The data is located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Aidan/data. In that folder, there are 4 folders (Hip 25Hz, Hip 100Hz, Wrist 25Hz, Wrist 100Hz) and one file (metadata.csv).

Datasets are as follows:

- 1. ”Wrist 100Hz”: One Axivity AX3 accelerometer, recording at 100 Hz and +/- 8g on the dominant wrist within a silicone wristband, with axes aligned as prescribed by the manufacturer. https://axivity.com/userguides/ax3/technical/#axis-alignment

- 2. ”Wrist 25Hz”: One Axivity AX3 accelerometer, recording at 25 Hz and +/- 8g on the dominant wrist within a silicone wristband, with axes aligned as prescribed by the manufacturer. https://axivity.com/userguides/ax3/technical/#axis-alignment

- 3. ”Hip 100Hz”: One Axivity AX3 accelerometer, recording at 100 Hz and +/- 8g clipped at the beltline, laterally above the dominant leg, with the +X axis approximately aligned in the superior direction, and the positive Y axis aligned to face anteriorly.

- 4. ”Hip 25Hz”: One Axivity AX3 accelerometer, recording at 100 Hz and +/- 8g clipped at the beltline, laterally above the dominant leg, with the +X axis approximately aligned in the superior direction, and the positive Y axis aligned to face anteriorly.

- 5. Participant sex and age range are provided in metadata.csv

Inside each of these folders, there are 39 files, one for each participant. The files are called as PX hip25.csv, for participant X (01, 02, 03, ...39) and hip25 is for the files inside Hip 25Hz.

The accelerometer data in each file has been resampled and calibrated using the Open Movement GUI software package. Within each CSV file, a step is annotated by a single ”1” at the approximate time of heel strike.

The primary purpose of this data collection is the development of step-counting algorithms, which, given just the raw accelerometer data, should be able to correctly estimate the number of steps. To measure how well it can do so, please use different statistics for this. This is particularly useful to compare a variety of algorithms and machine learning models, currently used for this purpose. With the concurrent collection of data from 2 different locations, we could also observe how the performance of these step-counting algorithms compares between the wrist and the hip. Using the metadata file, we can further explore if there are noted differences in different age groups or sexes.

Of particular interest to me is observing how step-counting algorithms are affected by the reduction in raw sampling frequency. While sampling at a lower frequency may cause the monitor to miss some high-frequency behavior, the vast majority of human movement occurs at far lower frequencies than the monitor can observe, sampling at 100Hz. Sampling data at a lower frequency can allow for longer periods of monitoring and requires less computing power, which is ideal, as long as it does not cause a significant drop in model performance.

Please make sure that in your project, you are counting steps, not windows. Given the limited dataset, use cross-validation to test the performance of the model.

Use state-of-the-art methods to analyze the data. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to

indicate whether the execution was successful or not. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data. You have access to 1 GPU and 10 cpus.

###### 5.8.2 Description of research output

Through two different iterations of prompts submitted to Denario for this dataset, seven different manuscripts were produced and analyzed. These seven manuscripts explored different research questions, with varying success, one of which, titled Wearable Step Counting: A Comparative Analysis of Deep Learning and Traditional Methods Highlighting Data Imbalance Challenges is shown in the Appendix A.8. For all of the manuscripts read, research questions explored the use of novel machine learning techniques to develop walking/step detection models. This investigation then compared how the developed models’ performance would be affected by various factors, such as subgroups of age and sex, device location or sampling frequency. The models used to detect walking/count steps, and read and process the data files used python. To evaluate the performance of the model, F1 or AUC statistics were used for walking detection, while mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was used for step counting.

The research questions explored by some manuscripts brought greater levels of novelty, investigating unique approaches for extracting gait fingerprints, or gait features, independent of device location. This research is particularly relevant for the development of step counting algorithms in phones, which could be located either in the hand, hence close to the wrist, or in the pocket, close to the hip. Unfortunately, for these more novel research questions, the model struggled to build insightful manuscripts, following this research question.

###### 5.8.3 Assessment of research output

For the processing of wearables data, we identified the following strengths and limitations:

###### Strengths:

- • Able to follow and understand the provided prompts: The Denario model followed the tasked prompt as expected. After noticing common errors in the first iteration and adjusting the prompt to avoid these errors in the following outputs, these errors were successfully avoided.
- • Opportunity to iteratively improve prompts: As previously noted, the first input to the Denario model did not match our expectations of output manuscripts, but explored useful ideas. These ideas and failures could then be used to better prompt the model in future attempts, iteratively producing better results.
- • Able to produce novel and useful research questions: Some of the research questions explored by the model provided a novel use of the dataset. Some of these insights have been stored as ideas for future fellowship applications.
- • Built on existing practices in the field: In many cases, the outputs of Denario are built on the use of existing models from published literature. In some cases, the research question involved the use of new approaches in machine learning, not yet applied to wearable data, but showed advanced domain knowledge in new machine learning approaches. In other cases, the evaluation metrics, and window segmenting approaches followed by Denario match that as standard in the wearable monitoring domain.

###### Limitations:

- • Use of jargon not relevant to the research question: It was noted that in several manuscripts produced by Denario, some methods or results chapters would consist of words and concepts that are relevant to the wearable monitoring space, but not relevant to the particular research question. One example manuscript explored how signal features differed between device locations, but results presented AUC scores, which would be expected to report the performance of a classification model, which was not developed in this manuscript.
- • Formatting of paper outputs: Some of the manuscripts lacked tables containing the performance of the models, which was instead solely presented in graphs. For other papers, the plots and tables had formatting issues, like using too small a font, tables overlapping with text, the lack of use of standard plotting techniques such as box plots and a lack of attaching some extra plots as supplementary material.

- • Reporting of data handling errors: In some cases, Denario failed to read some data files. Instead of the model failing to produce a manuscript, this was reported as part of the results; in some cases, a full section was created reporting these failures.
- • Preference for walking classification over step counting: Many of the models produced by Denario initially had a bias towards building 2-second walking detectors, rather than step counters, despite the prompt clearly indicating this was the intention of the study. This is likely due to this being a more common approach in literature, as there are very few step-counting datasets available.
- • Trade-off between novelty and manuscript quality: There was a noticeable trade-off between the novelty of the research questions, and the quality of the methods and results of the subsequent manuscript. This is likely because, for more novel research questions, there exists more limited literature regarding how to go about these investigations, leading to poorer decisions by the model.

In summary, Denario showed clear capabilities for wearable monitoring in the digital health domain, to produce useful research questions, conduct this research, and analyze the output data. It is noted, however, that there are quite a few limitations in the generation of reliable manuscripts. Overall, this encourages the use of this technology in earlier stages of the research process, to generate research questions, and to run exploratory analysis on datasets.

##### 5.9 Biophysics. Mechanistic understanding of protein folding pathways via dimensionality reduction methods

Characterizing protein folding and unfolding is one of the key challenges in theoretical and computational biophysics [68], as it requires an understanding of the associated high-dimensional energy landscapes and the kinetics of transitions between different metastable states. Long timescale simulations (microseconds and beyond) are therefore required to observe protein (un)folding events on an experimentally relevant timescale, leading to an understanding of the associated mechanistic pathways, identification of transient microstates, hidden allostery, and quantification of the kinetics of such processes. The N-terminal domain of ribosomal protein L9 (NTL9) is chosen as the model protein for this study since it undergoes microsecond-scale folding reversible folding with a well-characterized two-state folding mechanism. NTL9 has a well-characterized and experimentally validated folded structure that allows new algorithms and enhanced sampling schemes to reproduce the free energy landscape, intermediate ensembles, and rate constants. This suits the purpose of benchmarking studies due to its small size of 39 amino acid residues, absence of disulfide bonds, and lack of any complex post-translational modifications. This makes NTL9 an ideal candidate for developing new dimensional reduction methods to identify progress coordinates and understand mechanistic insights into protein folding and unfolding.

###### 5.9.1 Data generation

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed using the OpenMM engine [69] with the Amber14SB force field and the OBC2 implicit solvent model at 300 K, employing Langevin dynamics with a friction coefficient of 5 ps−1. The protein was subjected to energy minimization to remove steric clashes, followed by a 10 µs production run with an integration timestep of 2 fs. Protein coordinates were then saved every 2 ns for subsequent analyses.

###### 5.9.2 Project description

Denario was given the task to automate the post-simulation analysis of NTL9 protein (un)folding from MD simulation trajectories. The objective was to write a manuscript with detailed methodologies, dimensionality-reduction and clustering approaches, estimation of the free-energy landscape and kinetic rate constants (if possible), employ Markov state modeling to identify relevant low-dimensional progress coordinates that can characterize the mechanism of protein (un)folding, and establish scalable strategies for complex biomolecules. The input text to the system was this:

Input text

N-terminal domain of ribosomal protein L9 (NTL9) is a fast-folding protein domain that folds reversibly and is often used as a model to understand protein folding pathways. We aim to explore its unfolding thermodynamics and kinetics using an automated, generalizable pipeline. We have

a 10µs molecular dynamics (MD) simulation trajectory of the NTL9 protein undergoing folding. Simulation conditions for the trajectory obtained: Amber14SB force field with OBC2 implicit solvent, 300K Langevin dynamics, 2fs timestep, 2nm nonbonded cutoff, and H-bond constraints. Data: The simulation data is located at /mnt/home/aojha/AstroPilot/Project10. There are two files in the dataset, i.e., the simulation trajectory (an implicit-solvent 10µs MD trajectory consisting of 5000 frames saved every 2ns (ntl9 trajectory.dcd) and its corresponding topology PDB file (ntl9 topology.pdb). The simulation begins from an unfolded state of the NTL9 protein, while the topology file is a folded structure of the protein.

Motivation: Understanding how NTL9 unfolds and, by extension, how small single-domain proteins navigate their energy landscape reveals general principles of protein folding. Tracking down folding/unfolding pathways provides essential knowledge related to energy barriers, intermediates, transition states, and allostery involved in the process. We intend to build an analysis pipeline that breaks down local events, provides a mechanism for folding and unfolding events, describes the free energy profile for the process, and possibly the folding/unfolding kinetics. We also aim for this workflow to be generalizable for complex proteins or multi-domain systems, thereby addressing the gap between detailed MD simulations and high-level mechanistic insights.

###### Key Research Questions:

- 1. Data-driven collective coordinates: Can we identify interesting collective variables beyond the radius of gyration and root mean square deviation (RMSD) for profiling such folding/unfolding events? It will be interesting to compare the difference between using conventional collective variables (CVs) and generating new hidden CVs based on the simulation at hand. What are the dominant motions during folding/unfolding, and can we capture these motions with dimensionality reduction? There are numerous existing dimensional reduction methods. However, it would be interesting to see if we can keep increasing the complexity of such methods, starting from linear principal component analysis (PCA) and moving to spectral methods, such as diffusion maps, to explore non-linear manifold embedding. As we progress through the complexity level, it is expected that we will uncover more subtle unfolding pathways and intermediate microstates. Please provide a detailed description of each method, including analysis, figures, and tables. Create a hypothesis such as, “Linear PCA will capture the largest-scale structural separation (folded vs. unfolded), whereas a manifold embedding could reveal hidden intermediate microstates or pathways not evident in linear PCs.”
- 2. State Partitioning in low-dimensional space: Can we objectively identify distinct states (folded, intermediate, unfolded) from simulation trajectories? It would be interesting develop algorithms to identify the folded, unfolded, and intermediate states of the protein. Once trajectories are clustered using multiple algorithms, it will be useful to systematically visualize and compare their performance and derive best-practice guidelines for state identification.
- 3. Mechanisms of folding/unfolding: What local structural changes mark the onset of unfolding? How can we analyze such local changes and visualize them on a free energy landscape? Can we monitor the status of specific hydrogen bonds and native contacts throughout the trajectory, particularly those that stabilize the core, to determine when each bond first breaks? Can we construct a 2D free energy surface by binning the trajectory in the space of two most relevant CVs. This may highlight the free energy minima (states) and barriers between them. Then, using the cluster assignments from above, can we construct a simple Markov state model (MSM) or a transition matrix to estimate the rate constants for transitions?
- 4. Scalability and extension: How can this analysis pipeline be generalized to larger or multi-domain proteins? Can we propose strategies to manage longer trajectories and more complex proteins? For instance, using frame subsampling or incremental PCA to handle extremely long simulations, splitting the analysis by protein domain (which may be achieved by analyzing independent domain motions rather than a collective one), and employing graph-based representations of contacts or networks to capture inter-domain interactions. Please also discuss how to choose the dimensionality of the embedding or the number of

clusters in an automated way (e.g., using the percentage of variance, silhouette scores, etc.) for larger systems. It would be interesting to emphasize how each component of this pipeline can be adapted or scaled to ensure the approach remains efficient for complex proteins.

###### Manuscript Writing:

- 1. Title and Abstract: Emphasize generality, summarize the data, and highlight key analyses, such as the choice of CVs, clustering, free-energy mapping, and manifold embedding, while also highlighting mechanistic insights and extensibility.
- 2. Introduction: Present the NTL9 folding process in the broader context of protein folding/unfolding studies and identify the lack of scalable MD pipelines with proper references.
- 3. Methods: Provide step-by-step protocols for data loading, alignment, choice of CVs, clustering, manifold embedding, clustering, hydrogen-bond and dihedral analyses, free-energy surface calculation, kinetic estimates, and scalability strategies.
- 4. Results: Present the findings with well-annotated figures, tables, graphs, plots, and a detailed comparison and analysis.
- 5. Discussion: Interpret findings from the point of view of understanding the mechanism of protein folding pathways, compare linear vs. non-linear embeddings, assess the strengths and limitations of each step, and propose experimental validations (e.g., FRET, HDX) for complex proteins.
- 6. Conclusions and Outlook: Summarize core thermodynamic and kinetic insights, highlight the generality of the proposed workflow, and suggest future expansions (enhanced sampling, machine-learned CV discovery, allosteric network analyses).

Note: Do not use PyEMMA or any PyEMMA-based repositories. Instead, implement Markov modeling and implied-timescale analysis using scikit-learn, NumPy, and SciPy for matrix exponentials and eigen-decompositions, or any other lightweight MSM tools (e.g., msmtools).

###### 5.9.3 Assessment of research output

The generated paper, titled Comprehensive Kinetic and Free Energy Analysis of NTL9 Folding via Systematic Collective Variable Selection and Markov State Models, can be found in the Appendix A.9. The manuscript attempts to employ conventional collective variables (CVs) or order parameters, such as root mean square deviation (RMSD), radius of gyration, and native contacts, to capture the global structural motions of the protein folding pathway. It is interesting to note that principal component analysis (PCA), time-independent component analysis (tICA), and nonlinear diffusion maps were implemented successfully to construct Markov state models (MSMs). A hierarchical approach is implemented to select analysis methods, progressing from conventional CV choices to linear PCA, tICA, and diffusion map embedding, to identify slow modes. The 2D free energy surfaces projected on the CVs show the folded, intermediate, and unfolded states on the energy landscape, with distinct free energy minima, to explain the folding and unfolding pathways of the protein. For kinetic modeling, the manuscript validates the MSM by performing implied timescale convergence and Chapman-Kolmogorov tests to ensure the Markovian assumption holds. Interestingly, specific structural changes from the folded to the unfolded state of NTL9 are correlated with the loss of hydrogen bonds and native contacts, providing additional insights into the mechanistic pathways. In short, across all the different approaches, the manuscript consistently reported at least three protein states, namely folded, intermediate, and unfolded.

Although several methods are mentioned and employed in the study, the motivation or theory behind such approaches is lacking, making it difficult to follow without prior knowledge or implementation. There is an extensive use of technical jargon associated with each method (PCA, TICA, diffusion maps, MSMs), but it is hardly convincing or clear. For example, the study claims quantitative agreement of protein folding kinetics with experiments, but no such theoretical kinetic data or references are reported. Prior literature studies relevant to protein folding are absent, with little to no mention of existing benchmarking studies. For example, the manuscript does not refer to well-cited studies, such as the extensive MD simulations of NTL9 folding by Lindorff-Larsen et al. [70] or the MSM-based folding of NTL9 by Voelz et al [71]. The manuscript fails to report any statistical uncertainties or confidence intervals on estimations

of free energy differences, kinetic rate constants, or MFPTs. There is no discussion on error estimations, error bars, or Bayesian estimation of the transition matrix for MSM, which is an issue given that the manuscript claims an excellent agreement with the experiments. The study also fails to acknowledge the limitations of MD simulations, such as force field and sampling limitations, which are necessary for justifying analytical methods, including MSMs and enhanced dimensionality reduction approaches. The manuscript frequently cites figures and tables, but they are marked as ’not shown,’ disrupting the continuity, reproducibility, and interpretability for the reader.

Overall, the AI-generated manuscript on NTL9 protein folding serves as a clear proof-of-concept demonstrating the capability of LLM agents to generate scientific content. The methodology presented in the manuscript follows a logical and conventional scientific workflow. However, the scientific novelty remains limited and is not sufficiently communicated. The discussion and literature context provided in the manuscript are limited, and essential supporting data are absent, despite substantial claims being presented. Given these observations, the manuscript, in its current form, serves as a powerful demonstration but will require considerable manual refinement, contextual analysis, and validation to achieve adequate scientific communication with its readers.

##### 5.10 Neuroscience. Behavioral Cognitive Decline in Egyptian Fruit-Bats.

We also tested Denario on data from neuroscience. Specifically, we used it to study behavioral cognitive decline and its underlying brain changes in Egyptian fruit bats, which are known for their extreme longevity. We described in lots of detail the data and its characteristics in the input prompt:

Input text

We use a dataset of ∼40 Egyptian fruit bats (Rousettus aegyptiacus), with paired behavioral and MRI (diffusion tensor imaging - DTI) measures from the same subjects to investigate fruit bats’ cognitive and brain aging. Bats were aged based on their methylome profile.

###### Data Sources and Collection:

• Age determination: We followed Wilkinson et al. 2021 for methylome-based aging of the bats. DNA was extracted from wing biopsies using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit and protocol (QIAGEN Ltd., Germany). The extracted DNA was sent to an external laboratory (The Clock Foundation lab) for DNA methylation (DNAm) analysis.

Behavioral procedure - Our well-established foraging-box paradigm (Harten et al. 2021) served as an assay of age-related spatial cognitive decline. The setup consists of a large flight room with six opaque boxes with bowls of fruit placed inside them. Before the experiment, all bats underwent a habituation session. Here, groups of four bats were introduced to the same experimental apparatus that would be later used for individual testing but with adequate food and hydration available and accessible in all boxes (600 g of fresh fruit pieces and 200 ml of mango juice per box).

The test protocol consisted of three identical phases, each lasting three hours spread during two consecutive days. On the first day, bats completed two consecutive phases, while the final phase took place on the second day. In each phase, an individual bat foraged freely in the flight room containing six opaque boxes. Only one bowl allowed access to food (the correct box), while the others were blocked with a plastic mesh to avoid use of olfaction for box finding.

First phase - Individual testing started with a three-hour phase with one bowl accessible. After three hours, the bat was removed, and the correct bowl’s location was swapped randomly to a different box. The second phase- began immediately (2 minutes) after the swap and lasted three additional hours. This phase tested (among other measurements) the bats’ short-term memory of the previous location. After the second phase, the bat was removed from the setup for 18 hours.cIn the third phase (Long term memory) - the correct bowl was relocated to a third new location for the final three-hour phase.

Behavioral Data collection and analysis Each bat’s behavior was video recorded throughout the entire procedure. The videos were analyzed to identify when the bats landed on or entered the boxes.

- • Behavioral files. These are excel files with bat names located in /mnt/ceph/users/fvillaescusa/AstroPilot/Neuro/Yossi/data/Compressed data/behavioral data/<bat>.xslx, where <bat> is the name of the bat. All of the files are formatted uniformly, with a separate file per bat, each phase in a different sheet within the same file (test1/2/3), with each movement as a single row.

- • Actions in column F starting from row 7, were labeled ”L”=Land on box, ”E”=Box entry, ”F”=Box entry and took food. But for all purposes E and F are equal to us.
- • The correct box out of the 6 for the relevant phase is in 4D.
- • ”Video length” and ”first vid” in 1-2H can be ignored, we used them to calculate ”Absolute Time”.

- • ”Absolute Time” in 6B represents the time from the beginning of the current phase. While ”Time” in 6C is the corresponding timestamp in the video file.

- • ”in”+”out” in 6G and 6H is the timestamps in the video files of the bat’s movement in and out of the boxes. ”sum time” in 6I is the total time the bat spent in.
- • ”Part” in 6J is the video file number, can be ignored.
- • ”Comments” in 6K can be ignored.

MRI General Parameters

Bats underwent DTI MRI scans performed at Strauss MRI center located in Tel Aviv university, using a 7T/30 Bruker Biospec scanner and cross-coil configuration of quadrature coil and wholebody resonator. DTI was acquired using an echo-planar-imaging (EPI) pulse sequence, with 2 segments, TR/TE = 4000/19ms, D/d = 9/2.5ms with a b-value of 1000s/mm2 in 30 noncollinear directions and 3 b=0 images. DTI was conducted with inplane resolution of 0.5X0.5mm2, 34 axial/coronal slices (1mm, no gaps) covering the entire bat brain.

The DTI files are processed; we cut the surrounding and left only the brain (”skull stripping”) in the image. Then followed with stretching the image to be in uniform dimensions for analysis purposes. You can visually view the files using a free software such as ”MRIcron”. Diffusion files (DTI). Note that the DTI folder only contain the .nii files, not .bvec or .bval files

Additional background Bats as an aging model

Age determination: Laboratory animals are born in captivity, and therefore, their ages are accurately documented, while determination of the exact age of bats and other wild animal models has been a great challenge. Recent technological advancements have resulted in a minimally invasive method for determination of age. By analyzing epigenetic changes associated with age and longevity in the bat DNA methylome, it is now possible to determine their age with high accuracy while using only a small sample of the bat’s wing skin (Wilkinson et al. 2021).

One of the key advantages of bats in aging research is their remarkably long lifespan relative to their size. The remarkable longevity observed in many bat species, exemplified by the Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) which can surpass 25 years; a lifespan significantly exceeding expectations based on body size (up to 10 times longer) strongly implies a direct contribution from their unique biological characteristics (Brunet-Rossinni and Austad 2004; Foley et al. 2018; Lagunas-Rangel 2020; Podlutsky et al. 2005; Pollard et al. 2019). Moreover, bats’ distinctive immune system that provides resistance to a wide range of diseases, likely plays a pivotal role in their extended lifespans (Holtze et al. 2021; Kitsoulis, Baxevanis, and Abatzopoulos 2020; Weinberg and Yovel 2022) and resistance to chronic inflammation (Biga et al. 2024). It has been reported that in bats’ uniquely evolved immune system, some immune genes have been lost, others seemed to be under strong positive selection, with genes responsible for DNA damage checkpoints

and repair pathways exhibit accelerated positive selection (Weinberg and Yovel 2022). This sophisticated genetic architecture is further linked to observed resistance to cancer- bats rarely develop cancer, with some species as the Myotis pilosus named resistant to cancer (Hua et al. 2024). They poses exceptional ability to survive infections from life-threatening viruses like rabies with low mortality (George et al. 2011). Therefore, it is highly probable that these uniquely evolved traits in bats are some of the fundamental factors underpinning their exceptional longevity.

In 2005, the oldest recorded 41 years old Myotis brandtii bat was recaptured in the wild (Podlutsky et al. 2005). Myotis brandtii, was found to demonstrate notable qualities associated with longevity, including enhanced DNA repair mechanisms, balanced mitonuclear interactions, robust immune system function, remarkable resistance to oxidative stress, and effective telomere maintenance (Holtze et al. 2021).

Further research, such as (Stewart et al. 2021) found a great advantage the bat species Carollia perspicillata has to offer for cognitive aging research- their typical mammalian brain and neural organization, which shares striking similarities with that of primates and humans, distinguishing them from rodent models (Eilam-Altstadter et al. 2022; Stewart et al. 2021; Vernes 2017).

Importantly, bats are highly social animals, with various species such as the Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) living in close-knit colonies (Harten et al. 2018). Their extended lifespan, combined with residence in densely populated, vocally intense colonies, results in prolonged high-noise exposure, leading to age-related hearing loss consistent with typical mammalian patterns (Tarnovsky et al. 2023a).

These features make bats an intriguing model for investigating the mechanisms underlying harmful aging effects.

Given all the data and information above, please come up with a new and original idea for a project for a PhD thesis. For every step, make lots of plots and save the data you generate, as it may be used for other steps. When writing the code, write some lines to indicate whether the execution was successful or not. Join plots that are similar. Do not create dummy data.

The generated paper, titled Unraveling Brain Structural Correlates of Cognitive Aging and Resilience in Long-Lived Bats: An Integrated Study of Epigenetic Age and Spatial Memory, can be found on the Appendix A.10. The system nicely plotted data distributions, demonstrating its capacity to read and preprocess the available data. The system was able to identify relevant behavioral parameters, estimated them based on the raw behavioral data that it was fed with and ran the proper statistical tests (e.g., Mixed effect-Generalized Linear Models) to test how they change with age. It moreover performed QQ plots to validate that distribution of the model’s residuals. Some of the behavioral parameters identified by the system suggested a decline in spatial cognition with age in bats. The system attempted to connect brain and behavioral measurements by comparing models that explain cognitive performance by age alone or by age and brain volume combined. Indeed, it found a significant correlation between brain volume and one of the cognitive parameters. On the other hand, Denario did not perform outlier detection and removal prior to using the data, and it did not run a model comparison process.

When using brain scans, the system focused on estimating brain volume. Mean diffusivity maps are not the best MRI contrast images for estimating brain volume. Moreover, comparing brain volume across age is the most naive hypothesis and the system did not attempt to perform any analysis at the voxel level which could capture regional changes in brain structure with age. Indeed no significant correlation between brain volume and age was found.

##### 5.11 Materials Science. Confined Water Dynamics at Functionalized Graphene Interfaces

Understanding water and ion behavior in functionalized graphene nanochannels represents a fundamental challenge in materials science with direct applications to membrane separations, nanofluidic devices, and electrochemical systems[72, 73]. The ability to control interfacial water structure and dynamics through surface chemistry modifications could enable breakthrough technologies in water desalination, selective

ion transport, and energy storage[74]. However, the complex interplay between surface functionalization, coverage density, and electrolyte concentration creates a high-dimensional design space that is difficult to explore experimentally, making computational analysis essential for rational materials design.

The evaluation was based on our comprehensive molecular dynamics study (Hess et al. [75]), which systematically investigated how surface chemistry modulates confined electrolyte behavior—a critical question for advancing electrochemical and membrane technologies. This dataset comprised 91 MD trajectories spanning a three-dimensional parameter space: aqueous NaCl solutions (0-5 mol/kg) confined between graphene sheets functionalized with -COOH (carboxyl), -OH (hydroxyl), =O (carbonyl), and -CH3 (methyl) groups at three coverage levels (2.2%, 4.4%, 6.6%). Each trajectory contained 500 water molecules in a 15 ns production run at 300 K and 1 bar, with properties computed in two distinct regions: the interface (3-6 ˚A from the surface) and bulk (beyond 6 ˚A). Our published research revealed that functional group chemistry serves as the primary determinant of interfacial behavior, with polar hydrogenbonding groups (-COOH, -OH) creating highly structured interfaces with suppressed water diffusion

- (0.65-1.30 × 10−5 cm2/s), while nonpolar groups (=O, -CH3) maintained more diffuse, mobile profiles
- (1.15-1.35 × 10−5 cm2/s). Critically, we discovered that surface coverage acts as a secondary amplifier that scales the intensity of these effects without changing their fundamental nature—a distinction that persists across all electrolyte concentrations and provides a quantitative framework for designing surfaces with targeted transport properties.

We designed 10 prompts with systematically varying specificity to test Denario’s analytical capabilities across different levels of guidance. These ranged from broad conceptual queries like “How do you design surfaces for targeted water diffusion?” to explicit computational instructions with complete analysis workflows. With this comprehensive guidance, the system performed remarkably well in generating a complete research paper with appropriate methodology, analysis, and interpretation, though some minor quantitative inconsistencies and data completeness issues, discussed below, remained. One of the generated papers, titled Mapping Interfacial Water States on Functionalized Graphene: A Machine Learning-Augmented Approach to Uncover Design Principles for Tunable Water, can be found in the Appendix A.11.

Denario achieved perfect context understanding (100% success) and correctly identified analytical methods in 75% of cases. However, significant gaps emerged in quantitative accuracy and completeness. As shown in Figure 10, performance degraded systematically from context understanding through to novel insight generation, with the system generating only basic-level novel insights across all successful prompts.

###### 5.11.1 Assessment of Strengths

Denario demonstrated several notable capabilities in analyzing the confined water dataset, though these were primarily limited to foundational analytical tasks rather than advanced scientific discovery:

• Universal Context Recognition: The system achieved perfect scores (100%) in identifying the

problem domain across all 8 successful prompts, consistently recognizing the relevance to confined water dynamics, surface functionalization effects, and nanofluidic applications. This contextual awareness extended to understanding the multi-parameter nature of the problem (functional groups, coverage, concentration).

- • Methodological Competence: Denario correctly identified appropriate analytical methods in 75% of cases, including:

- – Mean squared displacement (MSD) calculations for diffusion coefficients
- – Density profile analysis for structural characterization
- – Hydrogen bond analysis for understanding water-surface interactions
- – Radial distribution functions for ion-water correlations

- • Qualitative Trend Recognition: The system successfully identified that hydrophilic groups (-COOH, -OH) would enhance water structuring and reduce mobility, while hydrophobic groups

(-CH3) and weakly polar groups (=O) would have minimal impact. This demonstrates an understanding of basic chemical principles and their connection to transport properties.
